raw_candidates.causal_claim: Ziegler et al. directly enabled Stiennon et al.'s leap by running the identical recipe (comparisons, Bradley-Terry reward model, PPO with KL penalty) at GPT-2 scale on the same TL;DR and CNN/DM tasks; Stiennon et al. state they follow this work and scale it up.
raw_candidates.definition: OpenAI paper (Ziegler et al., 2019): first fine-tuning of a pretrained LM (GPT-2) with a reward model trained from human comparisons, using PPO under a KL penalty to the pretrained model.
raw_candidates.name: Fine-tuning language models from human preferences (Ziegler et al.)
raw_candidates.source_title: Fine-Tuning Language Models from Human Preferences

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Christiano et al. directly enabled Stiennon et al.'s leap by inventing the preference-comparison reward-learning loop (learn a reward model from pairwise human comparisons, optimize it with RL) that the paper's method section adopts as its framework.
raw_candidates.definition: OpenAI/DeepMind paper (Christiano et al., 2017): trains agents from human comparisons between trajectory segments via a learned reward model, on MuJoCo and Atari.
raw_candidates.name: Deep RL from human preferences (Christiano et al.)
raw_candidates.source_title: Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences

raw_candidates.causal_claim: PPO directly enabled Stiennon et al.'s leap as the exact policy optimizer the paper runs against the reward model, with the KL-regularized reward fed into it.
raw_candidates.definition: Algorithm (Schulman et al., 2017): clipped-surrogate policy-gradient method that became the default optimizer for fine-tuning policies against learned rewards.
raw_candidates.name: PPO (proximal policy optimization)
raw_candidates.source_title: Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The Bradley-Terry model directly enabled Stiennon et al.'s leap because the reward model is trained with exactly its pairwise logistic loss on human comparisons.
raw_candidates.definition: Statistical model (Bradley & Terry, 1952): probability that one item beats another in a pairwise comparison is a logistic function of the difference of latent scores.
raw_candidates.name: Bradley-Terry model of paired comparisons
raw_candidates.source_title: Bradley-Terry model

raw_candidates.causal_claim: GPT-3 directly enabled Stiennon et al.'s leap because the policies, reward models, and supervised initializations are GPT-3 models of 1.3B-6.7B parameters; the paper states it uses large pretrained GPT-3 models.
raw_candidates.definition: OpenAI system (Brown et al., 2020): autoregressive LMs up to 175B parameters pretrained at scale, used by Stiennon et al. at 1.3B-6.7B sizes.
raw_candidates.name: Large-scale pretraining (GPT-3)
raw_candidates.source_title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners

raw_candidates.causal_claim: GPT-2 directly enabled Stiennon et al.'s leap as the base model class on which Ziegler et al. proved the recipe and from which the GPT-3 model family Stiennon et al. fine-tune descends.
raw_candidates.definition: OpenAI model (Radford et al., 2019): 1.5B-parameter Transformer LM whose zero-shot and fine-tuning behavior made large-scale LM fine-tuning the default substrate.
raw_candidates.name: GPT-2
raw_candidates.source_title: Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The Transformer directly enabled Stiennon et al.'s leap as the architecture of every model in the paper (policy, reward model, and the separate value network).
raw_candidates.definition: Architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017): self-attention sequence model that replaced recurrence as the default substrate for language models.
raw_candidates.name: Transformer architecture
raw_candidates.source_title: Attention Is All You Need

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Byte-pair encoding directly enabled Stiennon et al.'s leap because the policy's action space is BPE tokens: the paper treats each BPE token as one RL time step with reward delivered at the end of the sequence.
raw_candidates.definition: Tokenization method (Sennrich et al., 2016): subword segmentation by learned merge operations, adopted as the token unit of GPT-family models.
raw_candidates.name: Byte-pair encoding for NMT
raw_candidates.source_title: Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units

raw_candidates.causal_claim: GPT-1 directly enabled Stiennon et al.'s leap by founding the pretrain-then-fine-tune recipe whose RL variant the paper executes at GPT-3 scale.
raw_candidates.definition: OpenAI model (Radford et al., 2018): 117M Transformer decoder pretrained on BooksCorpus then fine-tuned per task.
raw_candidates.name: Generative pretraining (GPT-1)
raw_candidates.source_title: Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Bahdanau attention directly enabled Stiennon et al.'s leap as the mechanism inside the Transformer lineage whose encoder-decoder summarizers defined the field the paper's models replace.
raw_candidates.definition: Mechanism (Bahdanau et al., 2014): learned soft alignment between decoder states and encoder annotations in neural machine translation.
raw_candidates.name: Bahdanau attention
raw_candidates.source_title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Sequence-to-sequence learning directly enabled Stiennon et al.'s leap by creating the neural summarization paradigm (encode document, decode summary) whose supervised training the paper argues against and replaces.
raw_candidates.definition: Method (Sutskever et al., 2014): LSTM encoder-decoder mapping input sequences to output sequences, the template for neural abstractive summarization.
raw_candidates.name: Sequence-to-sequence learning
raw_candidates.source_title: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks

raw_candidates.causal_claim: LSTM directly enabled Stiennon et al.'s leap as the cell of the seq2seq summarizers (Paulus et al. and predecessors) that form the immediate prior state of the art the paper displaces.
raw_candidates.definition: Architecture (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997): gated recurrent cell with a constant error carousel, the sequence model of the pre-Transformer era.
raw_candidates.name: Long short-term memory (LSTM)
raw_candidates.source_title: Long Short-Term Memory

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Mikolov's RNNLM directly enabled Stiennon et al.'s leap by establishing the autoregressive neural language model whose maximum-likelihood training objective the paper identifies as the misaligned default.
raw_candidates.definition: Model class (Mikolov et al., 2010): recurrent neural network language models that beat n-gram models and founded neural LM practice.
raw_candidates.name: Recurrent neural network language model (Mikolov)
raw_candidates.source_title: Recurrent neural network based language model

raw_candidates.causal_claim: TAMER directly enabled Stiennon et al.'s leap by first showing an agent can be shaped by a learned model of human evaluative feedback rather than an environmental reward.
raw_candidates.definition: Framework (Knox & Stone, 2009): learns a model of human reward from evaluative feedback and uses it to shape an MDP agent's policy.
raw_candidates.name: TAMER framework (Knox & Stone)
raw_candidates.source_title: Interactively Shaping Agents via Human Reinforcement: The TAMER Framework

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Inverse RL directly enabled Stiennon et al.'s leap by founding reward learning: inferring a reward function from observed behavior or judgments instead of hand-specifying it.
raw_candidates.definition: Formulation (Ng & Russell, 2000): given an MDP and observed behavior, recover a reward function under which that behavior is optimal.
raw_candidates.name: Inverse reinforcement learning (Ng & Russell)
raw_candidates.source_title: Algorithms for Inverse Reinforcement Learning

raw_candidates.causal_claim: GAE directly enabled Stiennon et al.'s leap as the advantage estimator inside the PPO implementation used to train the summarization policies.
raw_candidates.definition: Method (Schulman et al., 2016): exponentially weighted advantage estimates trading bias against variance in policy-gradient methods.
raw_candidates.name: Generalized advantage estimation (GAE)
raw_candidates.source_title: High-Dimensional Continuous Control Using Generalized Advantage Estimation

raw_candidates.causal_claim: TRPO directly enabled Stiennon et al.'s leap by introducing the trust-region constraint on policy updates that PPO approximates and the paper's KL penalty echoes.
raw_candidates.definition: Algorithm (Schulman et al., 2015): policy optimization with a KL trust region guaranteeing monotonic improvement bounds.
raw_candidates.name: TRPO (trust region policy optimization)
raw_candidates.source_title: Trust Region Policy Optimization

raw_candidates.causal_claim: REINFORCE directly enabled Stiennon et al.'s leap as the original policy-gradient estimator from which the paper's PPO training descends.
raw_candidates.definition: Algorithm (Williams, 1992): gradient ascent on expected return using sampled episode returns, the founding policy-gradient method.
raw_candidates.name: REINFORCE (Williams)
raw_candidates.source_title: Simple Statistical Gradient-Following Algorithms for Connectionist Reinforcement Learning

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The policy gradient theorem directly enabled Stiennon et al.'s leap by giving the gradient of expected return that every optimizer in the paper's lineage implements.
raw_candidates.definition: Theorem (Sutton et al., 2000): the gradient of expected return with respect to policy parameters depends on the action-value function, not on state-distribution derivatives.
raw_candidates.name: Policy gradient theorem (Sutton et al.)
raw_candidates.source_title: Policy Gradient Methods for Reinforcement Learning with Function Approximation

raw_candidates.name: JSON (RFC 4627)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: JSON (RFC 4627) directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by fixing the six-type data model — objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, null — that every JSON Schema keyword annotates and validates
raw_candidates.source_title: The application/json Media Type for JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) RFC 4627
raw_candidates.definition: Crockford's 2006 RFC formalizing JSON as a lightweight text format for structured data derived from ECMAScript, providing the instance model JSON Schema describes.

raw_candidates.name: URI (RFC 3986)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: URI (RFC 3986) directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by supplying the URI-reference syntax and resolution rules used for schema identification and $ref-style referencing
raw_candidates.source_title: $ref (Draft 6)
raw_candidates.definition: The 2005 generic URI syntax standard whose absolute and relative references JSON Schema uses to point to other schemas, with JSON Pointer fragments.

raw_candidates.name: XML Schema Datatypes facets
raw_candidates.causal_claim: XML Schema Datatypes facets directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by providing the ingredient vocabulary of constraining facets — length, pattern, minimum, maximum, enumeration — recombined as JSON Schema keywords
raw_candidates.source_title: Comparing XML Schema Languages
raw_candidates.definition: W3C XML Schema Part 2's datatype hierarchy and facet system for restricting strings, numbers and dates, the direct ingredient set for JSON Schema's type and format keywords.

raw_candidates.name: ECMAScript (ECMA-262, 3rd edition)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: ECMAScript (ECMA-262, 3rd edition) directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by defining the object-literal notation and regular-expression syntax from which JSON and JSON Schema's pattern keyword derive
raw_candidates.source_title: @kernel-panic/jsv
raw_candidates.definition: The 1999 JavaScript language standard whose literal notation is JSON's subset and whose conventions early JSON Schema validators such as JSV were built on.

raw_candidates.name: URI Template (draft-gregorio-uritemplate)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: URI Template directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by giving its Hyper Schema drafts the templated-link machinery cited in draft-zyp-json-schema for hyperlink navigation and interaction control
raw_candidates.source_title: A JSON Media Type for Describing the Structure and Meaning of JSON Documents
raw_candidates.definition: Gregorio, Fielding, Hadley and Nottingham's in-progress URI Template draft, listed in JSON Schema draft-01's references for expanding templated URIs in hyperlinks.

raw_candidates.name: JSON Hyper Schema link relations (LRDD / Web linking)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: JSON Hyper Schema link relations directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by supplying the link-description component — describedby, self and full links — incorporated alongside core validation in the 2009 drafts
raw_candidates.source_title: A JSON Media Type for Describing the Structure and Meaning of JSON Documents
raw_candidates.definition: The hypermedia linking component split from core JSON Schema in draft-01, describing hyperlink structure of JSON documents on top of validation.

raw_candidates.name: W3C XML Schema (XSD)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: W3C XML Schema directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by providing the schema-language model — named types, occurrence and datatype restrictions declared in the format itself — that JSON Schema adapted from XML to JSON
raw_candidates.source_title: Comparing XML Schema Languages
raw_candidates.definition: The W3C's 2001 Recommendation for declaring XML structure and datatypes, the principal ancestor whose declarative validation model JSON Schema ported to JSON.

raw_candidates.name: RELAX NG
raw_candidates.causal_claim: RELAX NG directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by demonstrating a simpler, pattern-based, composable schema language as an alternative to XSD, a simplicity and composition model JSON Schema recombined for JSON
raw_candidates.source_title: Comparing XML Schema Languages
raw_candidates.definition: Clark and Murata's 2001 OASIS schema language, merging RELAX and TREX, based on patterns and regular tree grammars and later ISO/IEC 19757-2.

raw_candidates.name: XML Document Type Definition (DTD)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: XML Document Type Definition directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by establishing the original grammar-declaration ancestor — element/attribute declarations and required versus optional content — whose concepts schema languages including JSON Schema inherited
raw_candidates.source_title: XML Schema Validation: From RelaxNG to Modern JSON-LD
raw_candidates.definition: SGML-derived declarations inherited by XML 1.0 in 1998 for declaring document structure, with no real datatype system, the base of the schema-language lineage.

raw_candidates.name: TREX (Tree Regular Expressions for XML)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: TREX directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by proving a validation-only, modular pattern language simpler than XSD, one of the two parents merged into RELAX NG whose approach JSON Schema followed
raw_candidates.source_title: Even Experts Confounded by XML Schema
raw_candidates.definition: James Clark's December 2000 schema effort focused solely on validation of XML documents, simpler and more modular than W3C XML Schema.

raw_candidates.name: RELAX Core
raw_candidates.causal_claim: RELAX Core directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by showing a DTD-like but datatype-aware regular-language description could be easy to learn, the other parent merged into RELAX NG in the lineage JSON Schema adapted
raw_candidates.source_title: A Short History of XML Schema Languages (XML Schema)
raw_candidates.definition: Murata Makoto's March 2000 Japanese technical report, Regular Language Description for XML Core, designed as a simple alternative to XML Schema.

raw_candidates.name: Schematron
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Schematron directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by introducing assertion-based validation — rules asserting presence or absence of patterns — beyond grammar declaration, a constraint style JSON Schema's keywords extend
raw_candidates.source_title: Schematron
raw_candidates.definition: Rick Jelliffe's 1999 rule-based validation language using XPath assertions about XML trees, later ISO/IEC 19757-3, capable of constraints DTD and XSD cannot express.

raw_candidates.name: JSON
raw_candidates.causal_claim: JSON directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by being the format it annotates: Crockford's extraction of JavaScript object literals created the schemaless format that then needed a schema language of its own
raw_candidates.source_title: You Don't Know JSON: Part 1 - Origins, Evolution, and the Cracks in the Foundation
raw_candidates.definition: The data format popularized by Douglas Crockford from 2001, formalized in RFC 4627 in 2006, whose lack of built-in validation JSON Schema filled.

raw_candidates.name: Kris Zyp's first JSON Schema proposal (json.com)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Kris Zyp's first JSON Schema proposal directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by first formulating, on 2 October 2007, the named task of describing and validating JSON structure in JSON itself, two years before the IETF drafts
raw_candidates.source_title: What is JSON Schema?
raw_candidates.definition: Zyp's 2007 proposal submitted to json.com, the origin point the JSON Schema project itself dates its history to, preceding draft-zyp-json-schema-00 of December 2009.

raw_candidates.name: Ajax: A New Approach to Web Applications
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Ajax directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by creating the browser-to-server JSON data-exchange practice whose contracts — data fetched asynchronously and consumed by JavaScript — posed the need to declare expected JSON structure
raw_candidates.source_title: A brief history of Web APIs
raw_candidates.definition: Jesse James Garrett's February 2005 essay naming Ajax, after which developers shifted Ajax data exchange from XML to JSON, exploding web API use.

raw_candidates.name: Representational State Transfer (REST) dissertation
raw_candidates.causal_claim: REST directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by framing resources, uniform interfaces and self-descriptive messages for web APIs, the setting in which a machine-readable description of JSON payloads became a named need
raw_candidates.source_title: A brief history of Web APIs
raw_candidates.definition: Roy Fielding's 2000 doctoral dissertation coining REST, the architectural style later adopted for JSON-serving Web APIs.

raw_candidates.name: Kwalify
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Kwalify directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by posing and solving, in 2005, the task of validating YAML and JSON documents against a declarative schema written in the data format itself
raw_candidates.source_title: Kwalify Users' Guide (for Ruby and Java)
raw_candidates.definition: Makoto Kuwata's tiny schema validator for YAML and JSON, released by December 2005, self-described as smaller and poorer than RELAX NG or XML Schema.

raw_candidates.name: Rx (Simple, Extensible Schemata)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Rx directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by formulating validation for JSON/YAML-style data structures — not XML representations — as a distinct need, with core types for records, sequences, maps and combinations
raw_candidates.source_title: Rx: Simple, Extensible Schemata
raw_candidates.definition: Ricardo Signes's 2008 schema system for data structures matching JSON and YAML, written after XML-centric systems and Kwalify proved inadequate for that data model.

raw_candidates.name: James Clark's critique of W3C XML Schema
raw_candidates.causal_claim: James Clark's critique directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by naming XSD's core obstruction — 'too complicated' for anyone but huge companies — and launching TREX as the simpler validation-only response
raw_candidates.source_title: Even Experts Confounded by XML Schema
raw_candidates.definition: Clark's 2000-2001 public criticism that the W3C working group tried to accomplish too much, resulting in an overly complex specification, driving alternative lighter-weight schemas.

raw_candidates.name: Philip Wadler's XML Schema simplification comments (W3C Last Call)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Wadler's Last Call comments directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by formally diagnosing that XML Schema could be greatly simplified while extending its power, documenting the complexity obstruction inside the W3C process itself
raw_candidates.source_title: Last Word on Last Call - The Specification's Problems
raw_candidates.definition: Bell Labs' Philip Wadler's 2000 last-call comments prefaced by the warning that the current Schema proposal is complex and the XML community may not forgive it.

raw_candidates.name: Simon St. Laurent's intertwined-specifications critique
raw_candidates.causal_claim: St. Laurent's critique directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by naming the dependency-jungle obstruction — XSLT, XPath and XQuery all forced to implement XML Schema datatypes — that a standalone, minimal JSON schema language avoided
raw_candidates.source_title: Time to Refactor XML?
raw_candidates.definition: The February 2001 XML.com analysis reporting XML-DEV concern at mutual interdependence of W3C specifications centred on XML Schema datatypes and the Post Schema Validation Infoset.

raw_candidates.name: Murata Makoto's critique of W3C XML Schema
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Murata's critique directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by diagnosing, from inside the schema working group, that W3C's direction served database vendors over document validation, prompting his RELAX alternative lineage
raw_candidates.source_title: Even Experts Confounded by XML Schema
raw_candidates.definition: Murata, a schema working group member, started RELAX in late 2000 dissatisfied that the group focused more on benefits to vendors than on validation.

raw_candidates.name: Rick Jelliffe's critique of XSD (W3C please put XSD 1.1 on hold)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Jelliffe's 2009 critique directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by sustaining the published case, in the year of the first JSON Schema IETF draft, that XSD's complexity and surprises disqualified it as the web's data-contract language
raw_candidates.source_title: XML Schema (W3C)
raw_candidates.definition: Jelliffe's May 2009 critique, cited among the canonical summaries of XSD criticism alongside Clark's and Møller and Schwartzbach's, arguing the spec is several hundred pages and hard for non-experts.

raw_candidates.name: W3C XML Schema (XSD)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: W3C XML Schema directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by being the incumbent it was defined against: verbose, XML-syntax, overly complicated yet undeniably powerful validation that JSON developers had discarded with XML itself
raw_candidates.source_title: JSON Schema - It's About Time
raw_candidates.definition: The incumbent validation mechanism for XML from 2001, against whose Byzantine syntax and complexity JSON Schema positioned a JSON-native equivalent.

raw_candidates.name: Protocol Buffers
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Protocol Buffers directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by offering the rival schema-first answer of the moment — an IDL with code generation and binary encoding — against which JSON Schema defined itself as schema in JSON itself, with no codegen or binary wire format

raw_candidates.definition: Google's schema-based binary serialization system open-sourced in 2008, requiring a .proto IDL and generated classes in each language.

raw_candidates.name: Apache Thrift
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Apache Thrift directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by presenting the competing 2007 schema-plus-RPC model — IDL-defined structs with field tags — that framed the choice JSON APIs faced between compiled IDL contracts and declarative JSON validation
raw_candidates.source_title: Data Exchange Formats (Avro, Thrift, Protocol Buffers)

raw_candidates.name: Apache Avro
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Apache Avro directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by arriving in 2009 with JSON-written schemas for binary data and schema resolution, the closest contemporary rival use of JSON as a schema language, against which JSON Schema's pure validation-and-annotation scope was defined

raw_candidates.name: YAML 1.2
raw_candidates.causal_claim: YAML 1.2 directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by formalizing in October 2009 a rival human-readable data format that is a strict superset of JSON yet had no schema language of its own, sharpening JSON Schema's role as the validation layer for JSON-family data
raw_candidates.source_title: YAML
raw_candidates.definition: The 2009 third edition of YAML, first proposed by Clark Evans in 2001, designed as a human-friendly serialization language and official superset of JSON.

raw_candidates.name: ASN.1
raw_candidates.causal_claim: ASN.1 directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by standing as the older standardized IDL incumbent for describing protocol data, whose horrible tooling and bypass by history IETF discussion cited when arguing what a JSON-era schema should and should not be

raw_candidates.name: XML-Data
raw_candidates.causal_claim: XML-Data directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by trying first, in January 1998, to put DTD content into a schema vocabulary with datatypes — and being superseded and retired, clearing the lineage that ran through XSD to JSON Schema

raw_candidates.name: XML-Data Reduced (XDR)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: XDR directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by being the implemented-but-abandoned schema attempt — used by Microsoft's BizTalk, then retired in favour of W3C XML Schema — showing vendor schema dialects fail without a single standard
raw_candidates.source_title: A Short History of XML Schema Languages (XML Schema)
raw_candidates.definition: Microsoft and Edinburgh's July 1998 reduced subset of XML-Data, implemented by Microsoft and used by BizTalk, then superseded by W3C XML Schema.

raw_candidates.name: Document Content Description for XML (DCD)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: DCD directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by attempting in July 1998 to integrate XML-Data with RDF and make elements and attributes interchangeable — an attempt absorbed into XSD's references and then dropped
raw_candidates.source_title: Comparing XML Schema Languages

raw_candidates.name: Schema for Object-Oriented XML (SOX)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: SOX directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by trying an object-oriented schema language with interfaces and parameters in 1998-1999, a direction its sponsor Commerce One abandoned for W3C XML Schema

raw_candidates.definition: Veo Systems/Commerce One's September 1998 schema proposal, strongly influenced by OOP language design, widely used by Commerce One before being retired.

raw_candidates.name: Document Definition Markup Language (DDML / XSchema)

raw_candidates.name: Examplotron

raw_candidates.source_title: Comparing XML Schema Languages

raw_candidates.name: W3C XML Schema (XSD)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: W3C XML Schema directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by heading, in van der Vlist's lineage survey, the family — DTDs, XSD, RELAX NG, Schematron, Examplotron — from which histories derive JSON Schema's ancestry
raw_candidates.source_title: Comparing XML Schema Languages

raw_candidates.name: RELAX NG
raw_candidates.causal_claim: RELAX NG directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by being, in lineage surveys, the merger result of RELAX and TREX and the surviving simple alternative whose pattern model surveys place in JSON Schema's ancestry
raw_candidates.source_title: A Short History of XML Schema Languages (XML Schema)
raw_candidates.definition: Survey-listed product of the May 2001 merger of RELAX and TREX, co-edited by James Clark and Murata Makoto under an OASIS technical committee.

raw_candidates.name: XML Document Type Definition (DTD)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: DTD directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by being, in schema-language histories, the oldest widely supported ancestor from which every later schema family in the survey descends

raw_candidates.definition: Survey-listed oldest schema language, borrowed from SGML into XML, the first widely used method to formally define languages like HTML.

raw_candidates.name: Schematron
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Schematron directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by occupying, in comparative surveys, the non-grammar branch of the schema family tree — rule-based assertion — that complements the grammar branch JSON Schema mainly follows
raw_candidates.source_title: Comparing XML Schema Languages
raw_candidates.definition: Survey-listed non-typical schema language first proposed in September 1999 by Rick Jelliffe, defining validation rules using XPath expressions.

raw_candidates.name: JSON (RFC 4627)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: JSON (RFC 4627) directly enabled JSON Schema's leap by being, in histories of JSON, the 2006 formalization — following Crockford's 2001 discovery and 2005 Ajax adoption — that created the standardized format histories list as JSON Schema's immediate parent substrate
raw_candidates.source_title: You Don't Know JSON: Part 1 - Origins, Evolution, and the Cracks in the Foundation
raw_candidates.definition: History-listed milestone in JSON's evolution timeline: 2001 discovery, 2005 Ajax use, 2006 RFC 4627 formal standard, before JSON Schema drafts of 2009-2010.

raw_candidates.name: JavaScript object literal syntax
raw_candidates.causal_claim: JavaScript's object and array literal syntax directly enabled JSON (RFC 4627)'s leap by being the notation itself: the RFC defines JSON as a subset of that literal syntax, so the format needed no new grammar, only extraction and naming.
raw_candidates.source_title: JSON: discovered, not invented
raw_candidates.definition: The literal notation for objects and arrays built into JavaScript from its 1995 debut, later recognized as a self-contained data format.

raw_candidates.name: ECMAScript 3 object and array literal grammar
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The ECMA-262 3rd edition literal grammar directly enabled JSON's leap because RFC 4627 normatively defines its own grammar as a subset of exactly these productions - the text the format was carved from.
raw_candidates.source_title: Standard ECMA-262, 3rd edition
raw_candidates.definition: The object/array literal productions of ECMA-262 3rd edition (December 1999), the standardized text JSON's grammar subsets.

raw_candidates.name: Unicode
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The Unicode character model directly enabled JSON's leap because RFC 4627 defines a JSON string as a sequence of Unicode characters - the format's text is Unicode text by construction.
raw_candidates.source_title: UTF-8 and Unicode FAQ for Unix/Linux
raw_candidates.definition: The universal character set standard (version 1.0, 1991) whose characters are the atoms of JSON strings.

raw_candidates.name: UTF-8
raw_candidates.causal_claim: UTF-8 directly enabled JSON's leap by giving its Unicode text a byte encoding every web system could emit and detect; RFC 4627 section 3 builds its encoding detection on the UTF-8/16/32 patterns.
raw_candidates.source_title: UTF-8 and Unicode FAQ for Unix/Linux
raw_candidates.definition: Thompson and Pike's variable-width encoding of Unicode (designed 1992, presented 1993), the default wire encoding of JSON text.

raw_candidates.name: JavaScript
raw_candidates.causal_claim: JavaScript directly enabled JSON's leap as the single precursor the format was extracted from: Crockford's move was to take the language's data literals out of the language and standardize them alone.
raw_candidates.source_title: The beginning of JavaScript: Brendan Eich and ten days in 1995
raw_candidates.definition: Eich's 1995 browser language (Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript) whose literal subset JSON is.

raw_candidates.name: LiveScript
raw_candidates.causal_claim: LiveScript directly enabled JSON's leap as the shipping form of the source language: the literal notation reached the web under this name in Navigator 2.0 betas in September 1995.
raw_candidates.source_title: ECMAScript and the Future of JavaScript (book chapter)
raw_candidates.definition: The September-December 1995 shipping name of the language that became JavaScript.

raw_candidates.name: ECMA-262 first edition
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The first ECMAScript standard directly enabled JSON's leap by fixing the literal grammar in a vendor-neutral text that a format could later subset by reference.
raw_candidates.source_title: Standard ECMA-262 (history section)
raw_candidates.definition: The June 1997 Ecma standard that froze JavaScript's syntax, including its literals, into a citable specification.

raw_candidates.name: JScript
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Microsoft's JScript directly enabled JSON's leap by making the literal notation a two-vendor fact of the web platform rather than one browser's dialect, forcing the standardization JSON later subset.
raw_candidates.source_title: ECMAScript and the Future of JavaScript (book chapter)
raw_candidates.definition: Microsoft's 1996 reverse-engineered implementation of JavaScript for Internet Explorer 3.

raw_candidates.name: LiveWire (Netscape server-side JavaScript)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Server-side JavaScript directly enabled JSON's leap by putting the same literal notation on the server half of the wire, so the notation existed at both ends before it was a format.
raw_candidates.source_title: ECMAScript and the Future of JavaScript (book chapter)
raw_candidates.definition: Netscape's 1996 server-side JavaScript environment for Enterprise Server.

raw_candidates.name: XML-RPC
raw_candidates.causal_claim: XML-RPC directly enabled JSON's leap by first posing, in shipped form, the problem JSON answers better: simple typed data (structs, arrays, scalars) exchanged over plain HTTP.
raw_candidates.source_title: SOAP - Wikipedia
raw_candidates.definition: Winer's 1998 protocol for RPC over HTTP with XML-encoded typed values, subsetted from the 1998 SOAP design.

raw_candidates.name: REST (Fielding dissertation)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: REST directly enabled JSON's leap by re-posing web interaction as the transfer of resource representations, the problem form for which a minimal, language-shaped data representation was the missing piece.
raw_candidates.source_title: Fielding Dissertation: Abstract (UCI, 2000)
raw_candidates.definition: Fielding's 2000 architectural style: resources manipulated through representations over a uniform interface.

raw_candidates.name: YAML design brief
raw_candidates.causal_claim: YAML's design brief directly enabled JSON's leap by formulating the data-interchange problem in data terms - match the native data structures of dynamic languages, portable across languages, human-readable - in the XML-simplification community, weeks after the first JSON message.
raw_candidates.source_title: YAML - CodeArchaeology
raw_candidates.definition: Evans, Ingy and Ben-Kiki's May 2001 ranked design goals for a data-oriented serialization language, from the SML-DEV list.

raw_candidates.name: CORBA
raw_candidates.causal_claim: CORBA directly enabled JSON's leap by posing, a decade early and at enterprise scale, the language-neutral data-exchange problem (IDL types marshalled between unlike systems) that the web later needed answered cheaply.
raw_candidates.source_title: Common Object Request Broker Architecture - Wikipedia
raw_candidates.definition: OMG's 1991 distributed-object standard: IDL-defined types marshalled by an ORB between heterogeneous systems.

raw_candidates.name: ANSI X12 EDI
raw_candidates.causal_claim: EDI directly enabled JSON's leap by posing machine-to-machine structured data interchange as a standardization problem a generation earlier - the enterprise form of the problem the web inherited.
raw_candidates.source_title: From EDI To XML And UDDI: A Brief History Of Web Services
raw_candidates.definition: The 1979 ANSI standard family for electronic business documents exchanged between unlike computer systems.

raw_candidates.name: Programming with Circles, Triangles and Rectangles (Bierman & Meijer)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The Bierman-Meijer analysis directly enabled JSON's leap by naming and analyzing the obstruction: XSD and the XML data model do not fit object graphs, so data interchange needs a programming-language data model instead of a document model.
raw_candidates.source_title: Programming with Circles, Triangles and Rectangles (XML 2003)
raw_candidates.definition: The XML 2003 paper that analyzed the mismatch between XML/XSD data models and object-oriented type systems.

raw_candidates.name: Rethinking the Java SOAP Stack (Loughran & Smith)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Loughran and Smith's diagnosis directly enabled JSON's leap by arguing, from inside the web-services establishment, that any SOAP API relying on a perfect two-way mapping between XML data and native language objects is fundamentally flawed - the design JSON simply declines to attempt.
raw_candidates.source_title: Rethinking the Java SOAP Stack (HPL-2005-83)
raw_candidates.definition: The May 2005 HP Labs paper (HPL-2005-83) declaring JAX-RPC-style XML-object mapping fundamentally flawed.

raw_candidates.name: Dare Obasanjo's XSD-objects databinding critique
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Obasanjo's widely read critique directly enabled JSON's leap by documenting, construct by construct, the impedance mismatch between W3C XML Schema and typical object languages that made XML databinding toolkits fail.
raw_candidates.source_title: XML First (Stefan Tilkov's Blog, Feb 2005)
raw_candidates.definition: The 2004-05 essays by Microsoft's Dare Obasanjo on the XSD-to-objects impedance mismatch, quoted across the web-services blogosphere.

raw_candidates.name: W3C XML Schema Patterns for Databinding Working Group
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The W3C's databinding working group directly enabled JSON's leap by institutionalizing the diagnosis: the mismatch between XSD and programming languages was severe enough to charter a standards effort to catalogue the workarounds.
raw_candidates.source_title: When XML abstraction kills your web services (Lemire, May 2006)
raw_candidates.definition: The W3C working group chartered in 2005 to standardize mappings between XML Schema and programming-language objects.

raw_candidates.name: XML 1.0
raw_candidates.causal_claim: XML directly enabled JSON's leap as the incumbent it was defined against: every design goal in RFC 4627 (minimal, portable, textual, a subset of JavaScript) is a negation of the XML document stack's weight for data.
raw_candidates.source_title: You Don't Know JSON: Part 1 - Origins
raw_candidates.definition: The W3C's 1998 simplified-SGML markup standard that became the default format for data interchange by 2001.

raw_candidates.name: SOAP
raw_candidates.causal_claim: SOAP directly enabled JSON's leap as the incumbent object-access protocol whose envelope-plus-schema weight for a simple call defined the cost JSON's five-page format undercut.
raw_candidates.source_title: SOAP - Wikipedia
raw_candidates.definition: The XML messaging protocol (designed 1998; SOAP 1.1 published as a W3C Note in May 2000) that carried the WS-* web-services stack.

raw_candidates.name: Action Message Format (AMF)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: AMF directly enabled JSON's leap as the other incumbent for rich-client data: Macromedia's binary Flash Remoting format proved the demand for native-object data exchange, locked inside a proprietary plug-in that JSON's text subset escaped.
raw_candidates.source_title: Action Message Format - Wikipedia
raw_candidates.definition: Macromedia's binary serialization for Flash Remoting (introduced with Flash Player 6, 2002), exchanging ActionScript object graphs with servers.

raw_candidates.name: YAML
raw_candidates.causal_claim: YAML directly enabled JSON's leap as the sibling rival: the other data-oriented answer to XML, whose growing specification complexity left the minimal end of the design space to JSON.

raw_candidates.definition: Evans, Ingy and Ben-Kiki's data serialization language (first draft May 2001; version 1.0 in 2004), designed data-first against XML.

raw_candidates.name: CGI form encoding (application/x-www-form-urlencoded)

candidate.causal_claim: The Bierman-Meijer analysis directly enabled JSON's leap by naming and analyzing the obstruction: XSD and the XML data model do not fit object graphs, so data interchange needs a programming-language data model instead of a document model.
candidate.source_title: Programming with Circles, Triangles and Rectangles (XML 2003)
candidate.definition: The XML 2003 paper that analyzed the mismatch between XML/XSD data models and object-oriented type systems.

member_names: Programming with Circles, Triangles and Rectangles (Bierman & Meijer)

candidate.name: Rethinking the Java SOAP Stack (Loughran & Smith)
candidate.causal_claim: Loughran and Smith's diagnosis directly enabled JSON's leap by arguing, from inside the web-services establishment, that any SOAP API relying on a perfect two-way mapping between XML data and native language objects is fundamentally flawed - the design JSON simply declines to attempt.
candidate.source_title: Rethinking the Java SOAP Stack (HPL-2005-83)
candidate.definition: The May 2005 HP Labs paper (HPL-2005-83) declaring JAX-RPC-style XML-object mapping fundamentally flawed.

member_names: Rethinking the Java SOAP Stack (Loughran & Smith)

candidate.name: Dare Obasanjo's XSD-objects databinding critique
candidate.causal_claim: Obasanjo's widely read critique directly enabled JSON's leap by documenting, construct by construct, the impedance mismatch between W3C XML Schema and typical object languages that made XML databinding toolkits fail.
candidate.source_title: XML First (Stefan Tilkov's Blog, Feb 2005)
candidate.definition: The 2004-05 essays by Microsoft's Dare Obasanjo on the XSD-to-objects impedance mismatch, quoted across the web-services blogosphere.

candidate.name: W3C XML Schema Patterns for Databinding Working Group
candidate.causal_claim: The W3C's databinding working group directly enabled JSON's leap by institutionalizing the diagnosis: the mismatch between XSD and programming languages was severe enough to charter a standards effort to catalogue the workarounds.
candidate.source_title: When XML abstraction kills your web services (Lemire, May 2006)
candidate.definition: The W3C working group chartered in 2005 to standardize mappings between XML Schema and programming-language objects.

member_names: W3C XML Schema Patterns for Databinding Working Group

candidate.name: XML 1.0
candidate.causal_claim: XML directly enabled JSON's leap as the incumbent it was defined against: every design goal in RFC 4627 (minimal, portable, textual, a subset of JavaScript) is a negation of the XML document stack's weight for data.
candidate.source_title: You Don't Know JSON: Part 1 - Origins
candidate.definition: The W3C's 1998 simplified-SGML markup standard that became the default format for data interchange by 2001.

candidate.name: SOAP
candidate.causal_claim: SOAP directly enabled JSON's leap as the incumbent object-access protocol whose envelope-plus-schema weight for a simple call defined the cost JSON's five-page format undercut.
candidate.source_title: SOAP - Wikipedia
candidate.definition: The XML messaging protocol (designed 1998; SOAP 1.1 published as a W3C Note in May 2000) that carried the WS-* web-services stack.

candidate.name: Action Message Format (AMF)
candidate.causal_claim: AMF directly enabled JSON's leap as the other incumbent for rich-client data: Macromedia's binary Flash Remoting format proved the demand for native-object data exchange, locked inside a proprietary plug-in that JSON's text subset escaped.
candidate.source_title: Action Message Format - Wikipedia
candidate.definition: Macromedia's binary serialization for Flash Remoting (introduced with Flash Player 6, 2002), exchanging ActionScript object graphs with servers.

candidate.name: YAML
candidate.causal_claim: YAML directly enabled JSON's leap as the sibling rival: the other data-oriented answer to XML, whose growing specification complexity left the minimal end of the design space to JSON.
candidate.source_title: YAML - Wikipedia
candidate.definition: Evans, Ingy and Ben-Kiki's data serialization language (first draft May 2001; version 1.0 in 2004), designed data-first against XML.

candidate.name: CGI form encoding (application/x-www-form-urlencoded)
candidate.causal_claim: Form encoding directly enabled JSON's leap as the browser's actual built-in data channel that structured exchange displaced: flat name-value pairs were all a browser could natively send before script-driven exchange.
candidate.source_title: A brief history of Web APIs
candidate.definition: The HTML form submission encoding that was the web's only native browser-to-server data format through the 1990s.

candidate.name: DCOM
candidate.causal_claim: DCOM directly enabled JSON's leap as part of the incumbent distributed-object establishment whose platform-bound binary protocols defined what web data exchange had to escape.
candidate.source_title: From EDI To XML And UDDI: A Brief History Of Web Services
candidate.definition: Microsoft's 1996 distributed component object model for networked object invocation.

candidate.name: WDDX
candidate.causal_claim: WDDX directly enabled JSON's leap as the failed first attempt it replaced: Allaire's 1998 XML vocabulary for language-neutral data structures proved both the demand and the dead end of encoding data as documents.
candidate.source_title: Building Web Services with Java, Ch. 3: Evolution of XML Protocols
candidate.definition: Allaire's 1998 Web Distributed Data Exchange: data structures serialized as XML packets.

candidate.name: Rivest's S-expressions proposal (SEXP)
candidate.causal_claim: Rivest's SEXP draft directly enabled JSON's leap as the failed general-purpose attempt: a 1997 IETF proposal for exactly JSON's job (general, economical, transportable data notation) that never escaped its security-infrastructure niche.
candidate.source_title: S-Expressions (Rivest & Eastlake, Internet-Draft)
candidate.definition: Rivest's May 1997 Internet-Draft proposing S-expressions as a general data-interchange notation, from SDSI/SPKI.

candidate.name: Java object serialization
candidate.causal_claim: Java serialization directly enabled JSON's leap as the language-bound failure: JDK 1.1's built-in object serialization showed every platform wanted native-structure exchange, and that a single-language binary could not be the web's answer.
candidate.source_title: The Evolution of Data Formats: From CSV to JSON
candidate.definition: Java's 1997 built-in mechanism for turning object graphs into byte streams, readable only by Java.

candidate.name: Hidden-frame data passing
candidate.causal_claim: The hidden-frame technique directly enabled JSON's leap as the ad hoc practice it formalized: digiGroups, Noosh and State Software itself passed data into pages through invisible frames, and the first JSON message rode exactly this channel before the format had a name.
candidate.source_title: JSON - Wikipedia
candidate.definition: The circa-2000 practice of exchanging data between browser and server through hidden HTML frames without page reloads.

candidate.name: Cartoon Orbit plug-in messaging system
candidate.causal_claim: Cartoon Orbit's plug-in messaging directly enabled JSON's leap as the concrete failure at hand: the proprietary browser plug-in format used at Communities.com was the kind of system the State Software work had to escape, per the format's own origin account.
candidate.source_title: JSON - Wikipedia
candidate.definition: The proprietary messaging format of Communities.com's Cartoon Orbit trading game, recorded as a precursor to the JSON libraries.

candidate.name: ASN.1
candidate.causal_claim: ASN.1 directly enabled JSON's leap as the heavyweight ancestor that failed the web: the telecom world's complete data-description notation (1984) whose tooling weight showed what a data notation must not become.
candidate.source_title: The Evolution of Data Formats: From CSV to JSON
candidate.definition: The 1984 ITU/ISO abstract syntax notation for describing data structures independent of encoding.

candidate.name: OpenStep property lists
candidate.causal_claim: Property lists directly enabled JSON's leap as the platform-bound proof: NeXT's literal dictionary/array text format showed a programming-language-like literal notation works as a data format, inside one vendor's platform only.
candidate.source_title: The Evolution of Data Formats: From CSV to JSON
candidate.definition: NeXT/OpenStep's text format for dictionaries, arrays and strings used for preferences and serialization from 1994.

candidate.name: JAXB (XML data binding)
candidate.causal_claim: JAXB directly enabled JSON's leap as the failed industrial fix: Sun's standard for binding XML to Java objects embodied the mapping machinery whose flaws were being diagnosed in the same years, clearing the ground for a format needing no binding at all.
candidate.source_title: Rethinking the Java SOAP Stack (HPL-2005-83)
candidate.definition: Sun's Java Architecture for XML Binding (1.0, 2003), generating classes from schemas to marshal XML as objects.

candidate.name: Parsing data with eval()
candidate.causal_claim: eval()-parsing directly enabled JSON's leap as the recipe that made it instantly real: any browser could consume the format with zero new code because the language's own evaluator was the parser.
candidate.source_title: JSON: discovered, not invented
candidate.definition: The original JSON consumption recipe: evaluating a JSON text with JavaScript's eval() to obtain the data structure.

candidate.name: The json.org one-page grammar
candidate.causal_claim: The json.org page directly enabled JSON (RFC 4627)'s leap as the artifact the RFC codified: Crockford's one-page grammar (railroad diagrams; the 'for Good, not Evil' license) was the format's complete public specification for five years.
candidate.source_title: JSON - cloudparts.dev technology history
candidate.definition: Crockford's 2002 single-page publication of the JSON grammar at json.org, the format's only specification until the RFC.

candidate.name: Server-side emission of JavaScript literals
candidate.causal_claim: Server-side literal emission directly enabled JSON's leap as the production half of the recipe: any server language could produce the format by printing literals, which is how the first messages were generated at State Software.
candidate.source_title: The History of JSON and the People That Created It
candidate.definition: The practice of generating JavaScript object-literal text from server code as a data payload, from 2001.

candidate.name: SpiderMonkey
candidate.causal_claim: SpiderMonkey directly enabled JSON's leap as the programmability layer that made the literal notation executable fact: the first JavaScript engine implemented the object model whose literals JSON standardizes.
candidate.source_title: ECMAScript and the Future of JavaScript (book chapter)
candidate.definition: Netscape's original JavaScript engine (1996), the first implementation of the language whose literals JSON subsets.

candidate.name: Rhino (JavaScript in Java)
candidate.causal_claim: Rhino directly enabled JSON's leap by carrying the literal notation onto the server platform (Java) years before the format was named, evidence the notation already lived at both ends of the wire.
candidate.source_title: ECMAScript and the Future of JavaScript (book chapter)
candidate.definition: Netscape/Mozilla's 1997 implementation of JavaScript in Java, begun by Norris Boyd.

candidate.name: Netscape Navigator 2.0
candidate.causal_claim: Navigator 2.0 directly enabled JSON's leap as the shipping vehicle: the first browser with the interpreter built in, which put a literal-notation parser on every desk the format would ever reach.
candidate.source_title: The beginning of JavaScript: Brendan Eich and ten days in 1995
candidate.definition: The September 1995 browser release that first shipped JavaScript (as LiveScript).

candidate.name: XMLHttpRequest
candidate.causal_claim: XMLHttpRequest directly enabled JSON's leap as the tool the format was wielded with: Microsoft's 1999 browser API for asynchronous data fetching created the channel whose XML payload fit badly and whose script-native payload fit exactly.
candidate.source_title: JSON: discovered, not invented
candidate.definition: The browser API introduced in IE5 (March 1999) for Outlook Web Access, enabling asynchronous HTTP from script.

candidate.name: Java applets in the browser
candidate.causal_claim: Java applets directly enabled JSON's leap as the incumbent plug-in runtime its origin story is defined against: stateful browser-server communication was supposed to need applets or Flash, and JSON's premise was needing neither.
candidate.source_title: JSON - Wikipedia
candidate.definition: The 1995 plug-in technology for running Java bytecode inside web pages, the era's default rich-client channel.

candidate.name: Yahoo Web Services JSON output
candidate.causal_claim: Yahoo's JSON APIs directly enabled JSON (RFC 4627)'s leap by giving the format its first major-platform production use in December 2005, months before the RFC - the demand signal the formalization answered, with Crockford then inside Yahoo as its JavaScript architect.
candidate.source_title: JSON and Yahoo!'s JavaScript APIs (Simon Willison, 16 Dec 2005)
candidate.definition: Yahoo's December 2005 move to offer JSON as an output format across nearly all its Web Service APIs.

candidate.name: del.icio.us API
candidate.causal_claim: The del.icio.us API directly enabled JSON's leap as an early production proof that script-consumable data feeds (including callback-wrapped responses) were what developers actually wanted from web services.
candidate.source_title: JSON and Yahoo!'s JavaScript APIs (Simon Willison, 16 Dec 2005)
candidate.definition: The social-bookmarking service's early web API (2003-04), among the first to offer script-friendly data responses.

candidate.name: Flickr API
candidate.causal_claim: The Flickr API directly enabled JSON's leap as demand evidence: the 2004 API economy's flagship service exposed its data in XML, SOAP and REST forms whose friction was the market JSON's formalization addressed.
candidate.source_title: A brief history of Web APIs
candidate.definition: Flickr's 2004 public API offering SOAP, XML-RPC and REST endpoints for photo data.

candidate.name: Amazon Web Services
candidate.causal_claim: Amazon's 2002 web services directly enabled JSON's leap by creating the public-API market at scale - and by demonstrating, in XML, the payload weight that market would shed.
candidate.source_title: A brief history of Web APIs
candidate.definition: Amazon's July 2002 developer web services, among the first large public APIs, offered in SOAP and REST-query XML forms.

candidate.name: Google Web APIs (SOAP)
candidate.causal_claim: Google's SOAP-based Web APIs directly enabled JSON's leap as the era's most prestigious demonstration that web data wanted programmatic access - through a toolkit-and-WSDL channel whose heaviness was the counter-demonstration.
candidate.source_title: A brief history of Web APIs
candidate.definition: Google's April 2002 developer API exposing search via SOAP with a downloadable toolkit.

candidate.name: eBay API
candidate.causal_claim: eBay's 2000 API directly enabled JSON's leap as early demand evidence: one of the first large public APIs showed third-party data access was a market, in XML whose weight the market later shed.
candidate.source_title: A brief history of Web APIs
candidate.definition: eBay's November 2000 public API program, among the first large-scale web APIs.

candidate.name: ECMA-262 third edition
candidate.causal_claim: ECMA-262 3rd edition directly enabled JSON's leap as the standard the format implements a subset of: RFC 4627's own text anchors the grammar to this edition, making JSON an interface to a standard rather than to one vendor's language.
candidate.source_title: Standard ECMA-262, 3rd edition
candidate.definition: The December 1999 ECMAScript standard, the edition RFC 4627 cites as JSON's basis.

candidate.name: MIME media type framework
candidate.causal_claim: The MIME framework directly enabled JSON (RFC 4627)'s leap by supplying the registration machinery the RFC exists to operate: 'application/json' is a media type, and the RFC is a media-type registration with a grammar attached.
candidate.source_title: JSON - Wikipedia
candidate.definition: The 1996 RFC 2045-49 framework of media types under which application/json was registered.

candidate.name: HTTP/1.1
candidate.causal_claim: HTTP/1.1 directly enabled JSON's leap as the transport contract the format was designed inside: State Software's founding design held two HTTP connections open for duplex exchange, and JSON is the payload that design converged on.
candidate.source_title: JSON - Wikipedia
candidate.definition: The 1999 revision of the web's transfer protocol (RFC 2616), the channel of every early JSON exchange.

candidate.name: Lisp S-expressions
candidate.causal_claim: S-expressions directly enabled JSON's leap as the donor tradition's original literal data notation: Lisp established in 1960 that a language's own literal syntax can serve as a general data representation - the idea JSON re-instantiated for the web.
candidate.source_title: S-Expressions (Rivest & Eastlake, Internet-Draft)
candidate.definition: McCarthy's parenthesized list notation (1960), computing's first literal syntax used as a data format.

candidate.name: Scheme
candidate.causal_claim: Scheme directly enabled JSON's leap through the documented donor channel into JavaScript's design: Eich was hired to put a Scheme-like language in the browser, and its data-literal culture is part of what he shipped.
candidate.source_title: ECMAScript and the Future of JavaScript (book chapter)
candidate.definition: The minimalist Lisp dialect (1975) whose first-class functions and literal data Eich carried toward the browser language.

candidate.name: Self
candidate.causal_claim: Self directly enabled JSON's leap through the other documented donor channel: JavaScript's prototype object model - the objects whose literals JSON serializes - came from Self via Eich's design.
candidate.source_title: ECMAScript and the Future of JavaScript (book chapter)
candidate.definition: The prototype-based object language (1987, Ungar and Smith) that supplied JavaScript's object model.

candidate.name: Perl
candidate.causal_claim: Perl directly enabled JSON's leap as a parallel carrier of the literal-data culture: hashes and array literals dumped and re-eval'd (Data::Dumper, 1995) were the dynamic-language serialization practice that the era's data-format designs generalized.
candidate.source_title: YAML - CodeArchaeology
candidate.definition: Wall's 1987 dynamic language whose hash/array literals and dump/eval practice normalized literal-based serialization.

candidate.name: Python
candidate.causal_claim: Python directly enabled JSON's leap as the other mass carrier of the dict/list literal model: by 2001 the 'native data structures of dynamic languages' that data formats had to match were, concretely, Python's and JavaScript's literals.
candidate.source_title: YAML - CodeArchaeology
candidate.definition: Van Rossum's 1991 language whose dictionary and list literals are JSON's data model in another syntax.

candidate.name: Lua table constructors
candidate.causal_claim: Lua's table constructors directly enabled JSON's leap as the independent proof of concept: from 1993 a data-description syntax of nested constructors served as a working configuration and data format, showing a language's literals could be a format years before JSON.
candidate.source_title: Lua - Wikipedia
candidate.definition: Lua's single data-structuring mechanism (1993): constructor syntax for tables used as records, arrays and configuration data.

candidate.name: AWK associative arrays

candidate.source_title: The Evolution of Lua (HOPL 2007)
candidate.definition: The 1977 text-processing language whose associative arrays founded the dynamic-language dictionary tradition.

candidate.name: E programming language

candidate.source_title: The History of JSON and the People That Created It
candidate.definition: Electric Communities' distributed-object language (1997), built by Mark Miller, Crockford, Morningstar and others for secure message passing between endpoints.

candidate.name: Lucasfilm Habitat

candidate.source_title: The History of JSON and the People That Created It
candidate.definition: Lucasfilm's 1986 graphical multi-user world by Morningstar and Farmer, the first of its kind.

candidate.name: State Application Framework

candidate.definition: The web-application framework conceived by Morningstar at State Software (2001) for stateful browser applications.

candidate.source_title: JSON - Wikipedia
candidate.definition: The consulting company (founded March 2001, later Veil Networks) where JSON was specified and first used.

candidate.name: Electric Communities

candidate.definition: The virtual-worlds and distributed-objects company (mid-1990s) formed by Lucasfilm Habitat alumni including Morningstar and Crockford.

candidate.name: Communities.com
candidate.causal_claim: Communities.com directly enabled JSON's leap as the institution hosting the precursor: the Cartoon Orbit project's plug-in messaging, recorded as a precursor to the JSON libraries, ran there with the same people, immediately before State Software.

candidate.definition: The company whose Cartoon Orbit game used a precursor of the JSON libraries around 2000.

candidate.name: Netscape Communications

candidate.definition: The venture firm recorded as State Software's funder at its March 2001 founding.

candidate.definition: Google's April 2004 webmail, the first mass-market Ajax-style application.
