raw_candidates.causal_claim: The G80 card ships on a PCI Express x16 interface: the incorporated interconnect standard is what lets the device exist as a plug-in accelerator with 16 lanes of host bandwidth, replacing AGP in the design.
raw_candidates.definition: PCI-SIG's serial host interconnect (spec 1.0 in 2002-03), first shipped in graphics cards in 2004; the 8800 GTX is a PCIe 1.0 x16 card.
raw_candidates.name: PCI Express x16 interface
raw_candidates.source_title: GeForce 8800 GTX GPU specifications (TechPowerUp)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The G80 incorporates GDDR3 devices directly: 768 MB of GDDR3 on a 384-bit bus at 900 MHz is the memory system the chip's bandwidth (86.4 GB/s) is built from.
raw_candidates.definition: Graphics DDR3 SDRAM, specified by ATI with DRAM vendors from 2002 and later a JEDEC standard; first shipped on NVIDIA's GeForce FX 5700 Ultra in March 2004.
raw_candidates.name: GDDR3 SDRAM
raw_candidates.source_title: GDDR3 SDRAM (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The G80 incorporates a hardware thread scheduler (marketed as GigaThread) that issues vertex, geometry, pixel and compute threads onto the unified array - the scheduling mechanism inside the parent's design.
raw_candidates.definition: NVIDIA's name for the G80's hardware thread-management engine, part of the chip's own architecture as described in its November 2006 technical brief.
raw_candidates.name: GigaThread hardware thread scheduler
raw_candidates.source_title: NVIDIA GeForce 8800 GPU Architecture Technical Brief (TB-02787-001)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The G80 is a changed version of the Curie generation: it keeps the GeForce 7 pipeline organisation (texture units, ROPs, memory partitions) and replaces its split shader arrays with the unified array - the direct precursor it modified.
raw_candidates.definition: NVIDIA's 2005 flagship GPU (Curie architecture, TSMC 110 nm): 24 pixel pipelines and 8 vertex units, the peak of the split-pipeline design the G80 replaced.
raw_candidates.name: GeForce 7800 GTX (G70)
raw_candidates.source_title: GeForce 7 series (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The G80 extends the NV40 line two generations back: NV40 introduced Shader Model 3.0 programmability (dynamic branching, vertex texture fetch) whose limits the unified design answers.
raw_candidates.definition: NVIDIA's 2004 GPU (GeForce 6800), the first with Shader Model 3.0 and FP16 frame-buffer blending, on a split vertex/pixel architecture.
raw_candidates.name: GeForce 6800 (NV40)
raw_candidates.source_title: GeForce 6 series (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Xenos is the rival first draft of the parent's central idea: a unified shader array shipped a year earlier in a console, which the G80 answers on the PC with a scalar (not vector) unified design and a compute mode Xenos lacked.
raw_candidates.definition: ATI's custom Xbox 360 GPU (announced May 2005, shipped 22 Nov 2005): 48 unified vector shader units at 500 MHz on TSMC 90 nm, with a NEC eDRAM daughter die - the first unified shader architecture in a commercial GPU.
raw_candidates.name: ATI Xenos (Xbox 360 GPU)
raw_candidates.source_title: ATI Xenos: Xbox 360 Graphics Demystified (Beyond3D)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The NV30 line is the deeper ancestor whose failure mode (a split design bet against the DX9 template) disciplined the two generations that lead to the G80.
raw_candidates.definition: NVIDIA's 2003 CineFX GPU (GeForce FX 5800), a commercial and critical failure against ATI's R300, late and hot on a 130 nm process.
raw_candidates.name: GeForce FX (NV30)
raw_candidates.source_title: GeForce FX series (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The R300 set the template the whole lineage modifies: the first DirectX 9 programmable pipeline, against whose design every subsequent NVIDIA architecture (including the G80) positioned itself.
raw_candidates.definition: ATI's 2002 flagship (Radeon 9700 Pro), the first DirectX 9 / Shader Model 2.0 GPU, which took the performance lead and defined the programmable-pipeline era.
raw_candidates.name: Radeon 9700 Pro (R300)
raw_candidates.source_title: Radeon R300 series (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The original GeForce 256 is the lineage's root artifact: the first chip called a GPU, whose fixed-function T&L pipeline is the thing the G80's programmable unified array ultimately replaces.
raw_candidates.definition: NVIDIA's 1999 chip, marketed as the first GPU, with integrated transform and lighting - the fixed-function starting point of the GeForce architecture line.
raw_candidates.name: GeForce 256
raw_candidates.source_title: GeForce 256 (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The DirectX 10 problem was posed to NVIDIA years before either shipped: under the Windows Graphics Foundation name, Microsoft's re-posed requirement - one common shader core for all stages, a new geometry stage, guaranteed feature set - was the specification the G80's four-year design targeted, and the G80 served as the reference hardware for the API's development.
raw_candidates.definition: Microsoft's next-generation graphics API effort (WGF 2.0, later Direct3D 10), designed with hardware vendors from about 2002 and circulated to IHVs in draft form well before its November 2006 release alongside Windows Vista.
raw_candidates.name: Windows Graphics Foundation / Direct3D 10 specification effort
raw_candidates.source_title: Direct3D 10 architecture white paper (Microsoft)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The GPGPU community posed the problem the G80's compute mode answers: from about 2003, gpgpu.org and the early GPGPU papers formulated 'the GPU as a general-purpose coprocessor' as an explicit goal that graphics APIs could not serve.
raw_candidates.definition: The research community and web hub (gpgpu.org, from 2003) that collected the first wave of general-purpose GPU computing work and named the field.
raw_candidates.name: GPGPU problem formulation (gpgpu.org community)
raw_candidates.source_title: The Evolution of GPU Computing (Steve Scott, SC12)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Microsoft's Xbox 360 graphics brief posed the unified-shader problem in shipped form a year before the G80: a console GPU requirement, designed with ATI over about two years, that made dynamic load balancing across one shader array a product requirement.
raw_candidates.definition: Microsoft's 2003-era design requirement for its second console's graphics chip, executed by ATI as Xenos - the commission that first made a unified shader array a shipping product.
raw_candidates.name: Xbox 360 graphics design brief (Microsoft)
raw_candidates.source_title: Microsoft & ATI unveil Xbox 360 GPU (2005 reportage)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Inside NVIDIA, the design brief that produced the G80 was posed around 2002: over the four-year design, the observation that people were increasingly using graphics hardware for non-graphics work was turned into an explicit requirement - a direct computing mode rather than graphics in disguise (Kirk's retrospective account).
raw_candidates.definition: NVIDIA's internal G80 design requirement, as later described by chief scientist David Kirk: the chip was designed over roughly four years with general-purpose use as a stated goal.
raw_candidates.name: NVIDIA's GPGPU design requirement (the four-year G80 brief)
raw_candidates.source_title: Nvidia Takes Fresh Tack In PC Graphics (CRN, Nov 2006)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The diagnosis the unified array answers: in split pipelines, vertex and pixel units idle whenever a scene's load is unbalanced, so peak throughput is unreachable in principle - an inefficiency named in architecture analyses of the DX9 generation and in NVIDIA's own retrospective ('Outstanding performance with a unified shader design' is the brief's answer to it).
raw_candidates.definition: The analysed structural defect of separate vertex/pixel pipelines - static partitioning wastes whichever array the current workload does not need - documented in mid-2000s architecture analyses and retrospectives.
raw_candidates.name: Split-pipeline load-imbalance diagnosis
raw_candidates.source_title: NVIDIA Tesla: A Unified Graphics and Computing Architecture (Lindholm et al., IEEE Micro 2008)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The early GPGPU literature diagnosed exactly what the G80's compute hardware removes: no scatter, no integer operations, no shared memory or inter-thread communication, and programs forced to masquerade as rendering - the limitation list (Purcell et al. 2002 and successors) that the Tesla architecture's design answers point by point.
raw_candidates.definition: The 2002-2004 analyses of programmable graphics hardware as a computer (Purcell et al.'s ray-tracing work; Thompson et al.'s framework analysis) cataloguing the graphics API's limits for general computation.
raw_candidates.name: Early GPGPU limitation analyses
raw_candidates.source_title: The Evolution of GPU Computing (Steve Scott, SC12)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The scalar-efficiency argument is the diagnosis behind the G80's most distinctive choice: vec4 shader units waste most of their width on the scalar-heavy instruction mixes of real shaders, so a scalar unit at a higher clock beats a wider vector unit - the argument the Tesla design adopted against both its own predecessors and Xenos's 5-wide vectors.
raw_candidates.definition: The utilisation analysis of vector shader units under real instruction mixes, used in the Tesla architecture's rationale for scalar stream processors (Lindholm et al. 2008).
raw_candidates.name: Vector-unit underutilisation diagnosis (the scalar argument)
raw_candidates.source_title: Tesla (microarchitecture) (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The R580 was the incumbent the G80 displaced at launch: ATI's 48-pixel-shader split design held the high end through 2006, and the G80's reviews define its leap against it.
raw_candidates.definition: ATI's January 2006 flagship (Radeon X1900 XTX): 48 pixel shader units with a separate vertex array - the most powerful split-pipeline GPU ever shipped.
raw_candidates.name: Radeon X1900 XTX (R580)
raw_candidates.source_title: Radeon X1000 series (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The G71 was NVIDIA's own incumbent flagship in the G80's launch year - the product the 8800 GTX replaced in the line and the split-design endpoint inside the company.
raw_candidates.definition: NVIDIA's March 2006 flagship (GeForce 7900 GTX, 90 nm shrink of G70), the last and fastest of the split-pipeline GeForce designs.
raw_candidates.name: GeForce 7900 GTX (G71)
raw_candidates.source_title: GeForce 7 series (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The Cell was the rival throughput philosophy of the G80's exact moment: a heterogeneous CPU whose synergistic processors were the alternative answer to parallel throughput, locked in a console while the G80 shipped as a programmable PC part.
raw_candidates.definition: IBM/Sony/Toshiba's Broadband Engine (in PlayStation 3, November 2006): one Power core plus eight synergistic processing elements, the era's other bet on explicit parallel throughput.
raw_candidates.name: Cell Broadband Engine
raw_candidates.source_title: Cell (microprocessor) (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Ageia's PPU was the dedicated-accelerator incumbent the G80 absorbed: the 8800's launch positioning explicitly claimed geometry and physics processing on the GPU, against the separate physics card that had shipped months earlier.
raw_candidates.definition: Ageia's PhysX PPU (cards shipped March 2006), the first dedicated physics accelerator - the add-in model the G80's general-purpose array made unnecessary.
raw_candidates.name: Ageia PhysX PPU
raw_candidates.source_title: PhysX (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Intel's integrated graphics was the volume incumbent of the G80's era - the default 'GPU' most PCs shipped - defining by contrast the discrete high-end category the parent extended.
raw_candidates.definition: Intel's Graphics Media Accelerator 950 (2005), the integrated graphics of the Pentium 4 / early Core era, with no hardware vertex shaders.
raw_candidates.name: Intel GMA 950
raw_candidates.source_title: Intel GMA (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The R520 was ATI's shipping high end for most of the G80's final design year: a ring-bus split design whose documented limits (vertex/pixel partitioning, SM3.0 ceiling) are the state of the art the parent's leap is measured from.
raw_candidates.definition: ATI's October 2005 flagship (Radeon X1800 XT), a 90 nm split-pipeline design with a ring-bus memory controller.
raw_candidates.name: Radeon X1800 XT (R520)
raw_candidates.source_title: Radeon X1000 series (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The R400 is the negative space of the unified idea: ATI's own first attempt at a unified PC GPU was cancelled (its work reportedly fed the console design instead), showing the leap had been attempted and abandoned once before it shipped in Xenos and the G80.
raw_candidates.definition: ATI's cancelled circa-2003 PC GPU project, widely reported to have been the company's first unified-shader design, abandoned in favour of the R300-derived line.
raw_candidates.name: ATI R400 (cancelled unified GPU)
raw_candidates.source_title: ATI Xenos: Xbox 360 Graphics Demystified (Beyond3D)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The NV30 failure is the lineage's negative space inside NVIDIA: a late, hot, underperforming flagship whose fixes (process discipline, bandwidth, conservative clocks) shaped the NV40-G70-G80 design culture that produced the parent.
raw_candidates.definition: The GeForce FX 5800 launch failure (2003): late to market, beaten by ATI's R300, and withdrawn quickly - the company's defining product failure of the era.
raw_candidates.name: GeForce FX 5800 failure (NV30 launch)
raw_candidates.source_title: GeForce FX series (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Talisman is the older negative space: Microsoft's ambitious tiled-rendering architecture failed to ship as designed in the late 1990s, and its failure pushed the industry (and Microsoft's API line that leads to Direct3D 10) toward the immediate-mode programmable pipeline the G80 completes.
raw_candidates.definition: Microsoft's 1996-98 high-end rendering architecture programme (chunked, object-based rendering), cancelled without shipping as specified; its concepts resurfaced in later console and API design.
raw_candidates.name: Microsoft Talisman architecture
raw_candidates.source_title: Talisman (Microsoft) (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The G80 was physically produced on TSMC's 90 nm generation: 681 million transistors on a 484 mm2 die - the largest commercial GPU yet - was only buildable because that process generation existed at production scale.
raw_candidates.definition: TSMC's 90 nm CMOS generation (Nexsys), in production from 2004, used for the G80, Xenos and Cell alike - the process node of the parent's entire hardware generation.
raw_candidates.name: TSMC 90 nm process generation
raw_candidates.source_title: GeForce 8800 GTX GPU specifications (TechPowerUp)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The process generation the G80's own predecessor used: G70's move from 110 nm to the G71's 90 nm shrink is the immediate machine-generation step the G80's full 90 nm design extends.
raw_candidates.definition: TSMC's 110 nm generation, used by the G70 in 2005 before the line moved to 90 nm - the process step directly behind the parent's node.
raw_candidates.name: TSMC 110 nm process (G70 generation)
raw_candidates.source_title: GeForce 7 series (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The G80 shipped into PCIe-platform machines: the Intel 915/925 and nForce4 chipsets of 2004 were the host platforms whose x16 slots and chipsets the card's existence as a product presupposes.
raw_candidates.definition: The 2004 PCI Express platform generation (Intel Grantsdale/Alderwood, NVIDIA nForce4) that put x16 graphics slots into mainstream PCs two years before the parent.
raw_candidates.name: PCI Express platform chipsets (Intel 9xx / nForce4)
raw_candidates.source_title: PCI Express (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The process wielded to produce the parent is TSMC's 90 nm flow itself - copper interconnect, low-k dielectrics, 300 mm wafers - the manufacturing recipe whose yields forced the design's split into the main die plus a separate NV I/O chip.
raw_candidates.definition: The 90 nm manufacturing flow (193 nm lithography, copper/low-k interconnect, 300 mm wafers) as operated by TSMC for large GPU dies in 2005-06.
raw_candidates.name: TSMC 90 nm manufacturing flow (copper/low-k, 300 mm)
raw_candidates.source_title: GeForce 8 series (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The commercial EDA flow (synthesis, place-and-route, timing closure, DRC/LVS sign-off) is the procedure by which a 681-million-transistor design was produced at all in 2006 - wielded by NVIDIA's teams, not part of the artifact.
raw_candidates.definition: The Synopsys/Cadence-class digital design flow of the mid-2000s, the standard recipe for producing a large GPU tape-out.
raw_candidates.name: Commercial EDA design flow (synthesis to sign-off)
raw_candidates.source_title: Electronic design automation (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The two-chip strategy was a wielded yield recipe: at 90 nm, a single 686-million-transistor die was at the edge of feasible yield, so the design was split into the shader core and a small separate I/O die - a production decision recorded in the launch coverage.
raw_candidates.definition: NVIDIA's decision to implement the G80 as two chips (681M-transistor main die plus a ~5M-transistor NV I/O die) for yield feasibility on 90 nm.
raw_candidates.name: Two-die yield strategy (G80 core + NV I/O chip)
raw_candidates.source_title: GeForce 8 series (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Cg is the programmability layer the G80's shader hardware was expressed in before Direct3D 10: the C-like model (profiles, compiled to the hardware's stages) is the software form of the programmability the unified array generalises.
raw_candidates.definition: NVIDIA's C-like shading language (2002, with Microsoft), compiled to vertex/fragment programs for the hardware generations leading into the G80.
raw_candidates.name: Cg shading language
raw_candidates.source_title: Cg (programming language) (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: HLSL is the language layer of the API the G80 was designed against: Direct3D 10 made HLSL the only authoring language for its common shader core, so the hardware's programmability contract was written in HLSL terms.
raw_candidates.definition: Microsoft's High-Level Shader Language (shipped with DirectX 9 in 2002), the authoring language for all Direct3D shader models including Shader Model 4.0.
raw_candidates.name: HLSL (High-Level Shader Language)
raw_candidates.source_title: Using Shaders in Direct3D 10 (Microsoft Learn)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: GLSL made the same programmability available on the OpenGL side the G80 also implements: the card's unified array serves two shading-language ecosystems, and GLSL's 2004 standardisation is part of the software environment the hardware was designed into.
raw_candidates.definition: The OpenGL Shading Language, standardised as core in OpenGL 2.0 (2004) by the ARB, the second shading language of the parent's era.
raw_candidates.name: GLSL (OpenGL Shading Language)
raw_candidates.source_title: OpenGL Shading Language (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: BrookGPU is the programmability layer that demonstrated the demand the G80's compute mode serves: it ran general computation on pre-G80 cards through graphics APIs, and its author carried the model into NVIDIA in 2004, during the G80's design.
raw_candidates.definition: Stanford's stream-programming system (Buck et al., 2004) that compiled C-like kernels to graphics APIs on existing GPUs - the working proof that a market for GPU computing existed before the hardware for it did.
raw_candidates.name: BrookGPU stream programming system
raw_candidates.source_title: BrookGPU (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: ATI's Close To Metal was the rival programmability bet of the parent's exact season: a thin hardware-level interface announced as BrookGPU's ideas moved to ATI - evidence the programmability layer, not just the silicon, was contested ground in 2006.
raw_candidates.definition: ATI/AMD's low-level GPU computing interface (announced 2006), the competing answer to programming the hardware directly.
raw_candidates.name: Close To Metal (CTM)
raw_candidates.source_title: Close To Metal (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The G80 was built with the era's EDA tooling as off-the-shelf components: commercial synthesis, simulation and emulation tools are the software the design was literally assembled through.
raw_candidates.definition: The commercial tool suites (Synopsys, Cadence, Mentor) used for GPU design and verification in the mid-2000s.
raw_candidates.name: EDA tool suites (Synopsys / Cadence / Mentor)
raw_candidates.source_title: Electronic design automation (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: NVIDIA's unified driver is the software the G80 shipped inside: one driver architecture across the product line, the build-side framework whose assumptions (a single programmable pipeline) the unified hardware completes.
raw_candidates.definition: NVIDIA's Unified Driver Architecture (from 2001, extended for the GeForce 8 launch), one driver binary serving all its GPUs.
raw_candidates.name: NVIDIA Unified Driver Architecture
raw_candidates.source_title: Unified Driver Architecture (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: NVIDIA's own developer tools (FX Composer, PerfHUD) were the tooling its ecosystem - and its launch benchmarks - were built with: the shader-authoring environment that defined how the hardware's programmability was exercised before release.
raw_candidates.definition: NVIDIA's shader authoring and profiling tools (FX Composer from 2003, PerfHUD from 2005), distributed to developers building for its hardware.
raw_candidates.name: FX Composer / PerfHUD developer tools
raw_candidates.source_title: NVIDIA PerfHUD (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The G80's wafers were printed by the 193 nm lithography generation: ArF scanners are the equipment class that produced every 90 nm GPU, wielded by the foundry rather than part of the design.
raw_candidates.definition: Argon-fluoride 193 nm lithography scanners (ASML/Nikon) as operated in 90 nm production lines from about 2003.
raw_candidates.name: 193 nm ArF lithography scanners
raw_candidates.source_title: ArF lithography (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Volume test equipment is what made a 681M-transistor part a product: automated test systems characterised and binned the dies (the GTX/GTS split itself is a binning outcome).
raw_candidates.definition: Automated test equipment (Teradyne/Advantest class) for high-volume logic test and speed binning, as used in GPU production in the mid-2000s.
raw_candidates.name: Automated test equipment (ATE) for GPU binning
raw_candidates.source_title: Automatic test equipment (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Hardware emulation is the equipment class on which a design of the G80's size was functionally verified before tape-out - the pre-silicon rig the architecture was debugged on.
raw_candidates.definition: Emulation systems (Cadence Palladium class) used to verify large ASIC designs before silicon, standard practice for GPU programmes by the mid-2000s.
raw_candidates.name: Hardware emulation systems (Palladium class)
raw_candidates.source_title: Hardware emulation (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Direct3D 10 is the interface the parent implements: 'the industry's first fully unified architecture-based DirectX 10-compatible GPU' is the launch claim itself, and the chip served as the API's reference hardware - the standard and the silicon were developed against each other.

raw_candidates.name: Direct3D 10 specification
raw_candidates.source_title: API Features (Direct3D 10) (Microsoft Learn)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The PCI Express specification is the agreed interface the parent interoperates through: its x16 graphics slot is a PCI-SIG standard the card implements, not an NVIDIA invention.
raw_candidates.definition: PCI-SIG's PCI Express base specification (1.0a 2003, 1.1 2005), defining the serial lanes and x16 graphics connector the card uses.
raw_candidates.name: PCI Express base specification (PCI-SIG)
raw_candidates.source_title: PCI Express (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: GDDR3's status as an open, multi-vendor standard is what the G80's memory system interoperates through: any qualified vendor's devices (Samsung, Hynix, Qimonda, Micron) could populate the card.
raw_candidates.definition: The GDDR3 specification as an industry standard (ATI-led from 2002, later adopted by JEDEC), enabling multi-source supply of the memory devices.
raw_candidates.name: GDDR3 standard (ATI-led, JEDEC-adopted)
raw_candidates.source_title: GDDR3 SDRAM (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: OpenGL 2.0 is the second interface the parent implements: the card's programmability contract exists in both the Direct3D and OpenGL ecosystems, and its GLSL support is part of the launch specification.
raw_candidates.definition: The OpenGL 2.0 specification (September 2004), which made GLSL a core part of the API the G80 supports.
raw_candidates.name: OpenGL 2.0 specification
raw_candidates.source_title: OpenGL (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: DirectX 9.0c / Shader Model 3.0 is the interface generation the parent succeeds and remains compatible with: the G80's design had to run the entire DX9 library while adding the DX10 model - the backward-compatibility constraint is part of its design brief.
raw_candidates.definition: Microsoft's DirectX 9.0c (2004) with Shader Model 3.0, the incumbent API contract every 2006 GPU still had to satisfy.
raw_candidates.name: DirectX 9.0c / Shader Model 3.0
raw_candidates.source_title: DirectX (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: 3DMark06 was the measurement scheme of the parent's launch season: the benchmark against which the 8800 GTX's leap was registered and marketed in January 2006's suite, updated for SM3.0-era hardware.
raw_candidates.definition: Futuremark's January 2006 benchmark, the standard synthetic test of the DX9c generation against which the G80's launch performance was reported.
raw_candidates.name: 3DMark06
raw_candidates.source_title: 3DMark (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: 3DMark05 was the standing measurement scheme of the parent's design years: the score the G70 and R520 generations optimised against, and the baseline the G80's reviewers doubled.
raw_candidates.definition: Futuremark's 2004 benchmark for the DirectX 9 generation, the era's default GPU comparison metric.
raw_candidates.name: 3DMark05
raw_candidates.source_title: 3DMark (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Timedemo benchmarking in shipping games (Doom 3, Half-Life 2) was the era's ground-truth measurement practice: the reviews that registered the G80's leap ran game timedemos, not only synthetic suites.
raw_candidates.definition: The review practice (2004 onward) of benchmarking GPUs with recorded demos in Doom 3 and Half-Life 2, treated as the authoritative real-world metric.
raw_candidates.name: Game timedemo benchmarking practice (Doom 3 / Half-Life 2)
raw_candidates.source_title: Doom 3 (Wikipedia)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: PerfHUD is the instrument that made shader-pipeline behaviour observable during the parent's development era: per-stage utilisation readouts are how load imbalance - the parent's motivating diagnosis - was seen in practice.
raw_candidates.definition: NVIDIA's performance-analysis tool (2005) exposing GPU pipeline utilisation and bottlenecks frame by frame for developers on its hardware.

raw_candidates.name: Self (programming language)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Self directly enabled JavaScript's leap by supplying its object model: Eich took prototype-based delegation - objects inheriting from other objects, with no classes - from Self as one of the design's three named pillars.
raw_candidates.source_title: SELF: The Power of Simplicity (Ungar & Smith, OOPSLA 1987)
raw_candidates.definition: Ungar and Smith's prototype-based object-oriented language (OOPSLA 1987; public releases from Stanford from 1990, then Sun Labs), in which objects are slot collections that inherit by delegating to prototypes rather than instantiating classes.

raw_candidates.name: Scheme
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Scheme directly enabled JavaScript's leap by supplying its function semantics: first-class functions, closures and lexical scoping are the Scheme core Eich kept under the Java-like syntax.
raw_candidates.source_title: Scheme: An Interpreter for Extended Lambda Calculus (Sussman & Steele, 1975)
raw_candidates.definition: Sussman and Steele's minimalist Lisp dialect (MIT AI Memo 349, 1975), the first Lisp with lexical scoping and first-class closures as the language's foundation.

raw_candidates.name: HyperTalk
raw_candidates.causal_claim: HyperTalk directly enabled JavaScript's leap by supplying the interaction model: scripts written by non-programmers, attached to visible page objects and fired by events, which the browser language re-created for HTML documents.
raw_candidates.source_title: JavaScript: The First 20 Years (HOPL)
raw_candidates.definition: The scripting language of Apple's HyperCard (1987, by Dan Winkler), in which end users attached English-like event-handler scripts to cards and buttons.

raw_candidates.name: AWK
raw_candidates.causal_claim: AWK directly enabled JavaScript's leap as one of Eich's cited influences: its associative arrays and pattern-action text processing fed the new language's object-as-map and string handling for page data.
raw_candidates.source_title: JavaScript (Wikipedia)
raw_candidates.definition: Aho, Weinberger and Kernighan's Unix text-processing language (Bell Labs, 1977), built on associative arrays and pattern-action rules.

raw_candidates.name: Smalltalk-80
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Smalltalk-80 directly enabled JavaScript's leap by establishing the message-passing object model and live-object culture that Self simplified and Eich drew on.
raw_candidates.source_title: JavaScript: The First 20 Years (HOPL)
raw_candidates.definition: Xerox PARC's object-oriented language and environment (publicly released 1980), in which everything is an object and computation is message passing.

raw_candidates.name: Java (programming language)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Java directly enabled JavaScript's leap by supplying the syntax skin and marketing frame management mandated: the new language had to 'look like Java' while remaining a lightweight scripting companion.
raw_candidates.source_title: JavaScript (Wikipedia)
raw_candidates.definition: Sun Microsystems' class-based language, publicly launched in May 1995 with the HotJava browser and the applet model of downloadable code.

raw_candidates.name: Scheme
raw_candidates.causal_claim: JavaScript is the Scheme-embedding plan altered: Eich was hired to put Scheme in the browser, and the shipped language is that plan recombined - Scheme's semantics retained, its surface replaced under the look-like-Java mandate.
raw_candidates.source_title: Brendan Eich (Wikipedia)
raw_candidates.definition: Sussman and Steele's minimalist Lisp dialect (MIT AI Memo 349, 1975), the first Lisp with lexical scoping and first-class closures as the language's foundation.

raw_candidates.name: Self (programming language)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: JavaScript is Self's object model modified for the browser: Self's uniform slot and delegation machinery simplified into constructor functions plus a prototype property, small enough to implement in ten days.
raw_candidates.source_title: SELF: The Power of Simplicity (Ungar & Smith, OOPSLA 1987)
raw_candidates.definition: Ungar and Smith's prototype-based object-oriented language (OOPSLA 1987; public releases from Stanford from 1990, then Sun Labs), in which objects are slot collections that inherit by delegating to prototypes rather than instantiating classes.

raw_candidates.name: HyperTalk
raw_candidates.causal_claim: JavaScript is HyperTalk's card-scripting ancestor modified: the same event-handler scripts for non-programmers, moved from HyperCard stacks to HTML pages and given a C-like surface.
raw_candidates.source_title: JavaScript: The First 20 Years (HOPL)
raw_candidates.definition: The scripting language of Apple's HyperCard (1987, by Dan Winkler), in which end users attached English-like event-handler scripts to cards and buttons.

raw_candidates.name: HTML forms (in NCSA Mosaic)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: HTML forms posed the problem JavaScript answers: once pages could collect input (Mosaic, 1993), validating and reacting to that input without a server round-trip became the browser's missing capability - form validation was Mocha's canonical first use.
raw_candidates.source_title: 1993: CGI Scripts and Early Server-Side Web Programming (Cybercultural)
raw_candidates.definition: The fill-in form elements implemented in NCSA Mosaic (1993) and later standardized in HTML 2.0, which let pages submit user input to servers.

raw_candidates.name: Visual Basic
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Visual Basic posed the role JavaScript fills: a component-scripting language for non-specialists alongside a professional systems language - Netscape's Java-for-components / Mocha-for-scripters split was explicitly analogized to the C++ / Visual Basic pairing on Windows.
raw_candidates.source_title: History of JavaScript: From Netscape to ECMAScript (Code Carbon)
raw_candidates.definition: Microsoft's visual component-programming system (1991) that made application scripting by non-professional programmers a mass practice on Windows.

raw_candidates.name: HyperCard
raw_candidates.causal_claim: HyperCard posed the problem at mass scale: millions of non-programmers authoring interactive, scripted documents - the demand a browser scripting language had to meet for the web's documents.
raw_candidates.source_title: JavaScript: The First 20 Years (HOPL)
raw_candidates.definition: Apple's hypermedia authoring system (1987, Bill Atkinson), which put scripted interactive stacks in the hands of end users.

raw_candidates.name: ViolaWWW

raw_candidates.name: Elman recurrent network
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The parent's architecture is the Elman network trained as a language model: a simple recurrent network whose hidden layer is copied to context units and fed back, so the state summarizes an unbounded history - the component the 2010 model incorporates wholesale.
raw_candidates.source_title: Finding Structure in Time (Elman, 1990)
raw_candidates.definition: Jeffrey Elman's simple recurrent network (Cognitive Science, 1990): a feedforward network with a context layer copying the hidden state, giving the network a trainable memory of the recent past; its tasks were next-item prediction tasks, and it explicitly develops Jordan's 1986 proposal.

raw_candidates.name: Backpropagation through time
raw_candidates.causal_claim: BPTT is the training procedure the parent incorporates: the 2010 model is trained by unfolding the recurrent network through time and applying backpropagation - Werbos's 1990 formalization is the standard account the field trains by.
raw_candidates.source_title: Backpropagation Through Time (D2L)
raw_candidates.definition: Werbos's procedure (Proceedings of the IEEE, 1990) for training recurrent networks: unfold the network through time and apply backpropagation through the unfolded copies.

raw_candidates.name: Backpropagation (Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Backpropagation is the learning rule inside every weight update of the parent; the 2010 model's training is backpropagation specialized through time.
raw_candidates.source_title: Backpropagation Through Time (D2L)
raw_candidates.definition: The 1986 Nature paper's generalized delta rule - gradient descent on network error by chain-rule propagation - the learning algorithm of the connectionist era.

raw_candidates.name: Class-based n-gram models (Brown et al.)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The parent's output layer incorporates Brown clustering's factorization: words are grouped into classes and the model predicts class-then-word, the class-based decomposition the 2010 architecture uses to keep its output layer tractable.
raw_candidates.source_title: Class-Based n-gram Models of Natural Language (Brown et al., 1992)
raw_candidates.definition: Brown, Della Pietra, deSouza, Lai and Mercer's IBM method (Computational Linguistics 18(4), 1992): words clustered into classes by mutual information so that n-gram probabilities factor through the classes.

raw_candidates.name: Jordan network
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The Jordan network is the other founding recurrent design - outputs fed back as context - which Elman's 1990 paper explicitly develops from; the parent's recurrence concept descends from this pair.
raw_candidates.source_title: Finding Structure in Time (Elman, 1990)
raw_candidates.definition: Michael Jordan's recurrent architecture (1986) feeding the network's previous outputs back as context inputs - the proposal Elman's hidden-state recurrence explicitly develops.

raw_candidates.name: Neural probabilistic language model (Bengio et al.)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The parent is the feedforward neural LM modified by recurrence: Bengio et al. replaced n-gram counting with learned word embeddings and a neural probability function over a fixed window; Mikolov's move is to make the context the network's own recurrent state.
raw_candidates.source_title: Neural Probabilistic Language Models - explainer
raw_candidates.definition: Bengio, Ducharme, Vincent and Jauvin's model (JMLR, 2003): words embedded in a continuous vector space, a feedforward network estimating the next word's probability from a fixed-length window - the founding neural language model.

raw_candidates.name: Continuous space language models (Schwenk)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Schwenk's continuous-space LM is the direct ancestor in the speech-recognition line: the architecture (projection layer plus feedforward network) that the Brno group extended, and the comparison point the 2010 paper's own slides distinguish their feedforward setup from.
raw_candidates.source_title: Continuous Space Language Models and related work (Schwenk, MT Marathon 2010 / PBML 93)
raw_candidates.definition: Holger Schwenk's continuous space language model (Computer Speech & Language 21(3), 2007): a neural LM engineered for large-vocabulary speech recognition, whose projection-layer architecture became the field's reference design.

raw_candidates.name: Hierarchical probabilistic neural network language model (Morin & Bengio)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Morin and Bengio's hierarchical decomposition of the output vocabulary is the ancestor the 2010 paper cites (its reference [11]) for making neural LM output layers tractable - the problem the parent instead answers with class factorization.
raw_candidates.source_title: Recurrent Neural Network Based Language Model (Mikolov et al., Interspeech 2010)
raw_candidates.definition: Morin and Bengio's 2005 model arranging the vocabulary in a binary tree so next-word probability is a product of decisions along a path, cutting the output layer's cost.

raw_candidates.name: Shannon's prediction and entropy of printed English
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Shannon posed the problem the parent works on: predicting the next symbol of English text, with entropy as its measure - the 1951 guessing-game paper defines language modeling as a task.
raw_candidates.source_title: Prediction and Entropy of Printed English (Shannon, 1951)
raw_candidates.definition: Shannon's 1951 Bell System Technical Journal paper: the guessing-game experiment measuring how predictable the next letter of English is, bounding the entropy of printed English at roughly 0.6-1.3 bits per letter with 100 letters of context.

raw_candidates.name: DARPA CSR task definition (WSJ benchmark)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The CSR corpus design (Paul & Baker, 1992) posed the shared task: large-vocabulary continuous speech recognition on Wall Street Journal text, with fixed training data and NIST-administered benchmark tests - the arena the parent's word-error-rate claims are made in.
raw_candidates.source_title: ACL Data Collection Initiative / WSJ CSR corpus
raw_candidates.definition: The design (Paul & Baker, 1992) of the Wall Street Journal-based CSR corpus and its benchmark tests: a general-purpose, large-vocabulary, high-perplexity recognition task with shared data and centrally administered scoring.

raw_candidates.name: The curse of dimensionality diagnosis (Bengio et al.)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The 2003 paper's motivating diagnosis - discrete word histories make n-gram estimation collapse under data sparseness, because the number of possible contexts grows exponentially while observations do not - is the obstruction statement the whole neural-LM line, the parent included, is written against.
raw_candidates.source_title: Neural Probabilistic Language Models - explainer
raw_candidates.definition: The diagnosis stated in Bengio et al. (2003): language modeling suffers a curse of dimensionality - a word sequence's probability must generalize across an exponential space of histories from finite data - which continuous word representations were proposed to cure.

raw_candidates.name: Bengio, Simard & Frasconi on learning long-term dependencies
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The 1994 analysis diagnosed why recurrent training is hard - gradient descent struggles to learn long-term dependencies - the standing obstruction the parent's simple architecture and training regime had to live with.
raw_candidates.source_title: Backpropagation Through Time (D2L)
raw_candidates.definition: Bengio, Simard and Frasconi's 1994 analysis (IEEE Trans. Neural Networks) of the difficulty of learning long-term dependencies with gradient descent in recurrent networks.

raw_candidates.name: Hochreiter's 1991 diploma thesis analysis of vanishing and exploding gradients (Untersuchungen zu dynamischen neuronalen Netzen)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Hochreiter's 1991 diagnosis of vanishing and exploding gradients is the obstruction statement for all recurrent training; the parent's answer is pragmatic (simple architecture, truncated training) rather than the gated answer his own later work gave.
raw_candidates.source_title: Backpropagation Through Time (D2L)
raw_candidates.definition: Sepp Hochreiter's 1991 diploma thesis (TU Munich) identifying the vanishing/exploding gradient problem in recurrent networks - the diagnosis the LSTM design answers.

raw_candidates.name: Kneser-Ney smoothing
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Kneser-Ney is the incumbent the parent defines itself against: the parent paper's named baseline (KN5) and its interpolation partner - the strongest classical estimator, whose perplexity the recurrent model roughly halves.
raw_candidates.source_title: Improved Backing-Off for M-Gram Language Modeling (Kneser & Ney, 1995)
raw_candidates.definition: Kneser and Ney's smoothing (ICASSP 1995): absolute discounting plus a continuation-probability lower-order distribution - the strongest classical n-gram estimator.

raw_candidates.name: Katz backoff
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Katz backoff is the classical architecture the parent's mixtures replace: fall back to shorter contexts when longer ones are unobserved - the design the KN5 baseline itself builds on.
raw_candidates.source_title: Speech and Language Processing, Kneser-Ney appendix (Jurafsky & Martin)
raw_candidates.definition: Slava Katz's backoff scheme (1987): when a longer context is unobserved, fall back to shorter contexts with discounted probabilities.

raw_candidates.name: Stupid backoff and web-scale n-gram counts (Brants et al.)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Brants et al. is the scale-first rival: enormous count tables with a deliberately simple backoff, which the field's survey literature records as the web-scale tendency - the alternative the parent's compact recurrent model answers.
raw_candidates.source_title: Continuous Space Language Models and related work (Schwenk, MT Marathon 2010 / PBML 93)
raw_candidates.definition: Brants et al.'s 2007 demonstration that enormous count tables (Google's Web 1T 5-grams) with a deliberately simple backoff scheme beat sophisticated smoothing at web scale.

raw_candidates.name: Good-Turing estimation
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Good-Turing is the root of the incumbent's machinery: the estimate that unseen events' probability mass equals the proportion of events seen exactly once underlies every smoothing method the parent competes with.
raw_candidates.source_title: Empirical Estimates of Parameter Distributions (Chen thesis, incl. Good-Turing)
raw_candidates.definition: I.J. Good's elaboration (1953) of Turing's wartime estimator: the probability of unseen events is estimated from the count of events seen exactly once - the root of all smoothing.

raw_candidates.name: Deleted interpolation (Jelinek & Mercer)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Deleted interpolation is the incumbent's combination recipe: mixing n-gram estimates of different orders with estimated weights - the form the parent's own RNN-plus-KN mixtures inherit.
raw_candidates.source_title: Perplexity (AI Research Center glossary)
raw_candidates.definition: Jelinek and Mercer's deleted interpolation (1980): combining n-gram estimates of different orders with data-estimated weights, from IBM's speech recognition program.

raw_candidates.name: Long short-term memory (LSTM)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The LSTM is the road not taken inside the parent's own design space: the gated recurrent architecture existed for thirteen years, and the 2010 paper's claim is precisely that the SIMPLE recurrent network - not the gated one - suffices for language modeling at scale.
raw_candidates.source_title: Backpropagation Through Time (D2L)
raw_candidates.definition: Hochreiter and Schmidhuber's gated recurrent architecture (1997) preserving gradient flow over long spans with a constant error carousel - the era's engineered answer to recurrent training difficulty.

raw_candidates.name: Bidirectional recurrent neural networks
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The bidirectional RNN is the sibling recurrent design not used: reading the sequence in both directions, inapplicable to left-to-right prediction - its exclusion defines the parent's causal design choice.
raw_candidates.source_title: Backpropagation Through Time (D2L)
raw_candidates.definition: Schuster and Paliwal's bidirectional recurrent network (1997), running one recurrent layer forward and one backward over the sequence.

raw_candidates.name: Distributed representations (Hinton, McClelland & Rumelhart)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The parent's first component is imported whole from this chapter: a concept - here, a word - is represented not by a symbol but by a pattern of activity over many units, so similarity becomes proximity of vectors; the 2003 model learns exactly such a representation for each word.
raw_candidates.source_title: Geoffrey Hinton - Curriculum Vitae (publications list)
raw_candidates.definition: The Parallel Distributed Processing volume 1 chapter (1986) stating the connectionist representation doctrine: concepts as patterns of activation distributed over many units, similar concepts as nearby patterns.

raw_candidates.name: Learning distributed representations of concepts (Hinton)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The learning half of the doctrine: this paper showed distributed representations can be LEARNED by a network from examples rather than hand-designed - the parent learns its word vectors by training, following this demonstration.
raw_candidates.source_title: Geoffrey E. Hinton's Publications: Backpropagation
raw_candidates.definition: Hinton's 1986 Cognitive Science Society paper showing a network can learn distributed representations of concepts, reprinted in the PDP literature.

raw_candidates.name: Perceptron (Rosenblatt)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The parent's architecture descends from the perceptron line: layered adaptive units trained from examples; the multi-layer network computing the parent's probability function is this design's descendant.
raw_candidates.source_title: Geoffrey E. Hinton's Publications: Backpropagation
raw_candidates.definition: Frank Rosenblatt's perceptron (1958): a trainable layered network of threshold units - the ancestor artifact of every multi-layer network, the parent's included.

raw_candidates.name: Modeling high-dimensional discrete data with multi-layer neural networks (Bengio & Bengio)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The parent's own section 1.2 names this the prior demonstration: neural networks can model joint distributions of high-dimensional discrete variables by factorizing them into conditionals estimated by a multi-layer network - the 2003 paper applies exactly this recipe to word sequences.
raw_candidates.source_title: A Neural Probabilistic Language Model (Bengio, Ducharme & Vincent, NIPS 2000)
raw_candidates.definition: Yoshua and Samy Bengio's NIPS 12 paper (2000): an autoregressive multi-layer network modeling joint distributions over high-dimensional discrete variables; cited by the parent (with its journal companion) as its references [2]/[3].

raw_candidates.name: Taking on the curse of dimensionality in joint distributions using neural networks (S. Bengio & Y. Bengio)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The companion statement of the group's program: the curse in joint distributions is the named enemy and neural factorization the proposed weapon - the framing the parent inherits verbatim for language modeling.
raw_candidates.source_title: A Neural Probabilistic Language Model (Bengio, Ducharme & Vincent, NIPS 2000)
raw_candidates.definition: Samy and Yoshua Bengio's IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks paper (11(3):550-557, 2000) arguing neural networks can take on the curse of dimensionality in joint distributions.

raw_candidates.name: Sequential neural text compression (Schmidhuber & Heil)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The parent's section 1.2 acknowledges this line as related work: neural networks had already been used autoregressively on text (at character level, for compression) - a prior existence proof that a neural net can model text sequences probabilistically.
raw_candidates.source_title: Neural language models - the Schmidhuber priority case (retrospective survey)
raw_candidates.definition: Schmidhuber and Heil's neural text-compression work (NIPS 1994; IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks 1996): an autoregressive neural model predicting the next character, later pressed as a priority claim against the parent.

raw_candidates.name: Natural language processing with modular PDP models (Miikkulainen & Dyer)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: An early demonstration that distributed representations inside neural networks could process language structure (stories, case roles) - part of the prior neural-language record behind the parent's 'the idea is not new' acknowledgment.
raw_candidates.source_title: A Neural Probabilistic Language Model - An Explainer
raw_candidates.definition: Risto Miikkulainen and Michael Dyer's modular connectionist NLP work (book, 1991): networks with distributed representations processing sentences and stories.

raw_candidates.name: Maximum entropy language modeling (Rosenfeld)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The strongest non-neural generalization program of the era: maximum-entropy models integrated heterogeneous features (triggers, class information) into one exponential model - the alternative answer to sparsity against which the parent's learned-representation answer is positioned.
raw_candidates.source_title: Brief History of Language Modeling - from counting to attention
raw_candidates.definition: Ronald Rosenfeld's maximum-entropy language modeling program (from 1994-96): a unified exponential model combining n-gram counts with long-distance features.

raw_candidates.name: Prediction and entropy of printed English (Shannon)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Shannon posed the problem the parent works on: predict the next symbol of English and measure its entropy - the founding task definition of language modeling and the source of its measure.
raw_candidates.source_title: Brief History of Language Modeling - from counting to attention
raw_candidates.definition: Shannon's 1951 guessing-game experiments bounding the entropy of printed English - the founding statement of next-symbol prediction as a measurable task.

raw_candidates.name: Continuous speech recognition by statistical methods (Jelinek)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Jelinek's IBM program posed statistical language modeling as an engineering task inside speech recognition - the arena, and the trigram tradition, in which the parent's claims are made and measured.
raw_candidates.source_title: Brief History of Language Modeling - from counting to attention
raw_candidates.definition: Frederick Jelinek's 1976 IEEE paper founding the IBM statistical approach to speech recognition, in which the language model is a statistical component estimated from text.

raw_candidates.name: Curse of dimensionality (Bellman)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The diagnosis gets its hearing here (routed from RNNLM's expansion, session 12): the parent's abstract and first section name the curse of dimensionality as the intrinsic difficulty of its problem and define the contribution as fighting it; the term and the exponential-growth diagnosis are Bellman's coinage.
raw_candidates.source_title: Curse of dimensionality (Bellman's coinage)
raw_candidates.definition: Richard Bellman's coinage (Dynamic Programming, 1957; phrasing popularized in Adaptive Control Processes, 1961): the exponential growth of volume and state space with dimension that defeats tabular methods.

raw_candidates.name: Good-Turing estimation
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Good and Turing's estimate specified the unseen-events obstruction quantitatively - how much probability mass belongs to events never observed - the precise statistical form of the sparsity problem inside n-gram estimation.
raw_candidates.source_title: Brief History of Language Modeling - from counting to attention
raw_candidates.definition: The 1953 estimator (Turing's wartime method, published by I. J. Good) assigning probability mass to unseen events from the count of events seen exactly once - the statistical core of smoothing.

raw_candidates.name: Katz back-off
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The incumbent machinery the parent's introduction positions itself against: back-off trigram models (Katz, 1987) are named in the paper as the traditional approach, which generalizes only by concatenating very short sequences seen in training.
raw_candidates.source_title: A Neural Probabilistic Language Model (Bengio et al., JMLR 3, 2003)
raw_candidates.definition: Slava Katz's 1987 back-off estimator: use the longest context with a reliable count, discounted, and fall back to shorter contexts - the standard trigram machinery of the era.

raw_candidates.name: Deleted interpolation (Jelinek & Mercer)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Consumed, not merely compared: the parent's headline numbers are mixtures of the neural model with an interpolated trigram - remove deleted interpolation and the 252-perplexity headline result does not exist in its reported form.
raw_candidates.source_title: A Neural Probabilistic Language Model (Bengio et al., JMLR 3, 2003)
raw_candidates.definition: Jelinek and Mercer's 1980 smoothing method: blend n-gram estimates of several orders with weights fitted on held-out data - the mixture partner inside the parent's best reported results.

raw_candidates.name: Class-based n-gram models (Brown et al.)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The strongest incumbent in the parent's own table: the Brown-corpus headline is measured against the class-based back-off model with 500 classes (perplexity 312) - the counting tradition's own attempt to share strength across similar words.
raw_candidates.source_title: A Neural Probabilistic Language Model (Bengio et al., JMLR 3, 2003)
raw_candidates.definition: Brown, Della Pietra, deSouza, Lai and Mercer's method (Computational Linguistics, 1992): words clustered into classes so n-gram probabilities factor through the classes, sharing counts among similar words.

raw_candidates.name: A bit of progress in language modeling (Goodman)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The counting tradition's high-water mark, cited by the parent: Goodman showed how far combining many n-gram tricks goes - the combined state of the art the neural approach had to beat on its own terms.
raw_candidates.source_title: A Neural Probabilistic Language Model (Bengio et al., JMLR 3, 2003)
raw_candidates.definition: Joshua Goodman's 2001 synthesis of n-gram improvements (caching, clustering, skipping and more), cited by the parent as the counting approach's best combined form.

raw_candidates.name: Empirical study of smoothing techniques (Chen & Goodman)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The study that standardized which smoothing counts as state of the art - the baseline discipline the parent's comparison tables follow when they report modified Kneser-Ney numbers.
raw_candidates.source_title: A Neural Probabilistic Language Model (Bengio et al., JMLR 3, 2003)
raw_candidates.definition: Stanley Chen and Joshua Goodman's 1999 empirical comparison establishing the ranking of smoothing methods the field, and the parent's tables, use.

raw_candidates.name: Kneser-Ney smoothing
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The strongest single incumbent the parent is measured against: on AP News the best n-gram in the parent's table is the 5-gram Kneser-Ney back-off model (perplexity 117) - the number the neural model's 109 is reported against. (Already a node in this graph, admitted at RNNLM's expansion.)

raw_candidates.name: Conservative policy iteration (Kakade & Langford)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The parent's theoretical constitution, in its own text: the performance-difference identity is 'from Kakade & Langford 2002', the surrogate matches the true objective to first order '(see Kakade & Langford, 2002)', section 3 presents conservative policy iteration and its lower bound, and the parent's Theorem 1 is stated as the extension of that bound 'to general stochastic policies, rather than just mixture policies'.
raw_candidates.source_title: Approximately Optimal Approximate Reinforcement Learning (Kakade & Langford, ICML 2002)
raw_candidates.definition: Sham Kakade and John Langford's ICML 2002 paper: conservative policy iteration - update by mixing the current policy with an approximately greedy one, (1-alpha) pi + alpha pi' - with a guaranteed improvement bound, termination in a small number of steps, and an approximately optimal returned policy, none depending explicitly on state-space size.

raw_candidates.name: A Natural Policy Gradient (Kakade)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The parent's section 7: 'The natural policy gradient (Kakade, 2002) can be obtained as a special case of the update in Equation (12)' - the parent's practical algorithm is this paper's Fisher-metric step with the penalty replaced by a hard KL constraint, and its experiments run 'natural gradient, the classic natural policy gradient algorithm (Kakade, 2002)' as the principal baseline. (The paper appeared at NIPS 14 in 2001; the parent cites the 2002 proceedings year.)
raw_candidates.source_title: A Natural Policy Gradient (Kakade, NIPS 14)
raw_candidates.definition: Sham Kakade's NIPS 14 paper (2001): the natural (covariant) policy gradient - steepest descent under the Fisher information metric of the policy's distribution manifold, following Amari's natural gradient - shown to move toward the greedy action of a policy-iteration step under compatible function approximation.

raw_candidates.name: Policy gradient theorem (Sutton et al.)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The identity the whole method stands on: the parent's surrogate gradient equals the true objective's gradient at the current policy (its Equation 4), which is the policy gradient theorem's content - the reason a sample-estimated surrogate gradient is a policy gradient at all. (Already a node in this graph, admitted at PPO's expansion; proposed here so the link is judged on this parent's documents.)
raw_candidates.source_title: Trust Region Policy Optimization (Schulman et al., ICML 2015)
raw_candidates.definition: Sutton, McAllester, Singh and Mansour's policy gradient theorem (2000): the gradient of expected return with respect to policy parameters expressed through the action-value function and the score function, with compatible function approximation preserving the gradient.

raw_candidates.name: Natural gradient (Amari)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The geometric origin: Amari's natural gradient defines steepest descent by the Fisher information metric on the distribution manifold rather than by coordinates - the idea Kakade's paper (its reference [1]: 'As suggested by Amari, it is better to define a metric based not on the choice of coordinates but rather on the manifold') carries into policy space. The parent does not cite Amari.
raw_candidates.source_title: A Natural Policy Gradient (Kakade, NIPS 14)
raw_candidates.definition: Shun-ichi Amari's 'Natural gradient works efficiently in learning' (Neural Computation 10, 1998): gradient descent corrected by the Fisher information metric of the statistical manifold, making learning invariant to parameterization.

raw_candidates.name: Conservative policy iteration (Kakade & Langford)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Ancestor modified (cross-lens duplicate of the L1 proposal): the parent takes CPI's mixture-policy guarantee and replaces the mixture coefficient alpha with a divergence between general stochastic policies - the modification is the parent's Theorem 1.
raw_candidates.source_title: Approximately Optimal Approximate Reinforcement Learning (Kakade & Langford, ICML 2002)
raw_candidates.definition: Kakade and Langford's conservative policy iteration (ICML 2002): mixture updates with an explicit improvement lower bound.

raw_candidates.name: Natural actor-critic (Peters & Schaal)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: In the parent's section 4 list of similar updates (Bagnell & Schneider 2003; Peters & Schaal 2008b; Peters et al. 2010) and cited for the single-path method's applicability to physical systems: the natural-gradient line's actor-critic form, estimating the Fisher-preconditioned gradient with a learned critic.
raw_candidates.source_title: Trust Region Policy Optimization (Schulman et al., ICML 2015)
raw_candidates.definition: Jan Peters and Stefan Schaal's natural actor-critic (Neurocomputing, 2008): an actor-critic algorithm whose actor follows the natural gradient, with the compatible critic estimated by least-squares temporal differencing.

raw_candidates.name: Covariant policy search (Bagnell & Schneider)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The other early form of the natural-gradient update, in the parent's section 4 list; the REPS paper records its distinct clarification - that Kakade's Fisher constraint 'can be seen as a Taylor expansion of the loss of information or relative entropy between the path distributions' - as the key insight of the KL-constraint line.

raw_candidates.definition: J. Andrew Bagnell and Jeff Schneider's covariant policy search (IJCAI 2003): policy search following the covariant (natural) gradient, with the observation that the Fisher-metric constraint is a second-order expansion of relative entropy between trajectory distributions.

raw_candidates.causal_claim: The estimation line behind the parent's single-path variant: the parent's section 5.1 says its sampling scheme 'is the one that is typically used for policy gradient estimation (Bartlett & Baxter, 2011)' - the GPOMDP tradition of estimating the policy gradient from single trajectories.

raw_candidates.definition: Peter Bartlett and Jonathan Baxter's infinite-horizon policy-gradient estimation work (the GPOMDP line, 2000-01): unbiased gradient estimates for average-reward policies from a single sample path.

raw_candidates.source_title: Approximately Optimal Approximate Reinforcement Learning (Kakade & Langford, ICML 2002)
raw_candidates.definition: Kakade and Langford's ICML 2002 paper posing guaranteed policy improvement as a bounded-step problem.

raw_candidates.definition: Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis's approximate policy iteration tradition (Neuro-Dynamic Programming, 1996): alternating approximate policy evaluation and greedy improvement with sampled value functions.

raw_candidates.name: Relative entropy policy search (Peters, Mülling & Altun)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The closest KL-constraint predecessor: REPS maximizes return subject to a bound on the relative entropy between old and new policy distributions, with an exact dual update. The parent's section 7 discusses it directly: 'REPS constrains the state-action marginals p(s,a), while TRPO constrains the conditionals p(a|s). Unlike REPS, our approach does not require a costly nonlinear optimization in the inner loop.' REPS's own text credits Bagnell & Schneider (2003) for first suggesting constraining information loss.
raw_candidates.source_title: Relative Entropy Policy Search (Peters, Mülling & Altun, AAAI 2010)
raw_candidates.definition: Jan Peters, Katharina Mülling and Yasemin Altun's relative entropy policy search (AAAI 2010): policy search maximizing expected return subject to a KL (information-loss) bound between the old and new state-action distributions, solved exactly through a convex dual.

raw_candidates.name: Guided policy search (Levine & Abbeel)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The co-author's own immediately prior KL-constraint practice: constrained GPS imposes a KL-divergence constraint between old and new trajectory distributions so local linear models stay valid. The parent's section 7: 'Levine and Abbeel (2014) also use a KL divergence constraint, but its purpose is to encourage the policy not to stray from regions where the estimated dynamics model is valid, while we do not attempt to estimate the system dynamics explicitly.'
raw_candidates.source_title: Learning Neural Network Policies with Guided Policy Search under Unknown Dynamics (Levine & Abbeel, NIPS 2014)
raw_candidates.definition: Sergey Levine and Pieter Abbeel's guided policy search under unknown dynamics (NIPS 2014): iteratively refitted local linear models optimize trajectory distributions under a KL constraint between successive trajectory distributions, then distill them into a general policy.

raw_candidates.name: Safe policy iteration (Pirotta et al.)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The parallel descendant of the same ancestor, in the parent's section 7: 'Pirotta et al. (2013) also build on and generalize Kakade and Langford's results, and they derive different algorithms from the ones here.'
raw_candidates.source_title: Trust Region Policy Optimization (Schulman et al., ICML 2015)
raw_candidates.definition: Matteo Pirotta, Marcello Restelli, Alessandra Pecorino and Daniele Calandriello's safe policy iteration work (ICML 2013): improvement-guaranteed policy iteration generalizing Kakade & Langford's conservative updates.

raw_candidates.name: Conjugate gradient method (Hestenes & Stiefel)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The wielded solver of the practical algorithm: the parent's section 6 - 'We use the conjugate gradient algorithm followed by a line search' - and its Appendix C solve the Fisher-system Ax = b by conjugate gradient without forming the matrix, the computational core that makes the constrained update feasible at tens of thousands of parameters.
raw_candidates.source_title: Trust Region Policy Optimization (Schulman et al., ICML 2015)
raw_candidates.definition: Magnus Hestenes and Eduard Stiefel's conjugate gradient method (1952): iterative solution of symmetric positive-definite linear systems by conjugate search directions, needing only matrix-vector products.

raw_candidates.name: Fast exact multiplication by the Hessian (Pearlmutter)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The wielded trick inside the solver: the parent's Appendix C computes Fisher-vector products analytically so conjugate gradient can run; the technique class - exact curvature-vector products without forming the matrix - is Pearlmutter's.
raw_candidates.source_title: Trust Region Policy Optimization (Schulman et al., ICML 2015)
raw_candidates.definition: Barak Pearlmutter's fast exact multiplication by the Hessian (Neural Computation, 1994): computing Hessian-vector products at the cost of a gradient evaluation, the enabling trick for matrix-free second-order methods.

raw_candidates.name: MuJoCo (Todorov, Erez & Tassa)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The consumed instrument of the headline locomotion results: the parent's section 8.1 - 'We conducted the robotic locomotion experiments using the MuJoCo simulator (Todorov et al., 2012)' - swimmer, hopper and walker, whose contact discontinuities are the paper's difficulty claim; its acknowledgments thank Todorov and Tassa 'for providing the MuJoCo simulator'.
raw_candidates.source_title: MuJoCo: A physics engine for model-based control (Todorov, Erez & Tassa, IROS 2012) - abstract
raw_candidates.definition: Emanuel Todorov, Tom Erez and Yuval Tassa's MuJoCo (IROS 2012): a physics engine tailored to model-based control, with smooth contact dynamics in generalized coordinates and dynamics evaluations fast enough for sampling-based control (about 400,000 evaluations per second on a 12-core machine for an 18-dof humanoid).

raw_candidates.name: Arcade Learning Environment (Bellemare et al.)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The consumed instrument of the Atari half: the parent's games were 'made available through the Arcade Learning Environment (Bellemare et al., 2013)', with preprocessing following Mnih et al. (2013) - the platform whose protocol defines the comparison in its Table 1.
raw_candidates.source_title: Reinforcement Learning Benchmarks (ALE and MuJoCo as the field's testbeds)
raw_candidates.definition: Marc Bellemare, Yavar Naddaf, Joel Veness and Michael Bowling's Arcade Learning Environment (JAIR, 2013): the Atari 2600 evaluation platform and methodology for general agents, with results on more than 55 games - the standard pixel-control testbed of the deep-RL era.

raw_candidates.name: Trust region methods in numerical optimization (Conn, Gould & Toint)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The name and frame import: 'trust region' is numerical optimization's term (canonically Conn, Gould and Toint's 2000 monograph) for optimizing a local model inside a region where it is trusted - the frame the parent's title announces ('We proposed and analyzed trust region methods for optimizing stochastic control policies'). The parent's reference list contains no trust-region optimization text; the import, if any, is of the frame, not a cited mechanism.
raw_candidates.source_title: Trust Region Policy Optimization (Schulman et al., ICML 2015)
raw_candidates.definition: Andrew Conn, Nicholas Gould and Philippe Toint's Trust Region Methods (SIAM, 2000): the canonical account of optimization by successive local models minimized within a trusted radius - the source field of the parent's title concept.

raw_candidates.name: KL divergence (Kullback & Leibler)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The measure the constraint is stated in: the parent defines D_KL, converts its total-variation theorem to a KL bound via Pinsker's inequality, and constrains mean KL in the practical algorithm - the divergence itself is Kullback and Leibler's 1951 definition, a constituent of the parent's statement.
raw_candidates.source_title: Trust Region Policy Optimization (Schulman et al., ICML 2015)
raw_candidates.definition: Solomon Kullback and Richard Leibler's divergence (1951): the expected log-likelihood ratio between two distributions - the information-theoretic distance the parent's trust region is a ball in.

raw_candidates.name: Fisher information (Rao)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The metric inside the practical algorithm: the parent constructs 'the Fisher information matrix (FIM) by analytically computing the Hessian of the KL divergence' and solves against it; the Fisher information itself is Rao's 1945 object, reaching the parent inside the natural-gradient formulation.
raw_candidates.source_title: Fisher information (the metric behind the natural gradient and the TRPO constraint)
raw_candidates.definition: The Fisher information (R. A. Fisher's concept, given its geometric role by C. R. Rao, 1945): the expected outer product of the score, equal to the negative expected Hessian of the log-likelihood - the local quadratic form of KL divergence and the metric of the natural gradient.

raw_candidates.source_title: Trust Region Policy Optimization (Schulman et al., ICML 2015)
raw_candidates.definition: David Hunter and Kenneth Lange's account of minorization-maximization (MM) algorithms (2004): optimization by iteratively maximizing a minorizing surrogate - the family (including EM) to which the parent assigns its Algorithm 1.

raw_candidates.name: Smalltalk-76
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The parent's own prior state and direct ancestor: Ingalls's POPL 1978 paper presents the first modern Smalltalk - objects communicating by messages, descriptions organized into classes, subclassing with inheritance, a compiled representation and a virtual memory - and its architecture is the one that 'endures in Smalltalk-80'. The parent is this system consolidated into the release version and published as a complete definition.
raw_candidates.source_title: The Smalltalk-76 Programming System: Design and Implementation (Ingalls, POPL 1978)
raw_candidates.definition: Smalltalk-76 (Xerox PARC Learning Research Group, designed by Dan Ingalls, 1976; published as 'The Smalltalk-76 Programming System: Design and Implementation', POPL 1978): the first Smalltalk in modern form - classes holding representation and methods, subclassing/inheritance, message sending, compiled bytecodes, automatic storage management - running interactively on the Alto.

raw_candidates.name: Simula 67
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The class concept itself, named by the parent's own book: the preface to Goldberg & Robson (1983) states that Smalltalk-80 is based on ideas from the Simula language (and on the visions of Kay). Kay's history treats Simula as one of the formative conceptions of the sixties. (Heard at Self's expansion and rejected there as mediated via this node; its own hearing is here, as that record directs.)
raw_candidates.source_title: Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard: The Inventors of Object-Oriented Programming (CompHist)
raw_candidates.definition: Simula 67 (Ole-Johan Dahl, Bjorn Myhrhaug and Kristen Nygaard, Norwegian Computing Center; presented 1967, 'SIMULA 67 Common Base Language' 1968): the first class concept - a class as a template bundling data with procedures, objects as its instances, subclassing by class prefixing (inheritance), virtual procedures, and garbage collection - built as a generalization of ALGOL 60 for simulation.

raw_candidates.name: Lisp
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Kay's dedication in 'The Early History of Smalltalk' names LISP among 'the four great programming conceptions of the sixties' parented into Smalltalk: the interactive, image-based, garbage-collected symbolic computing that Smalltalk's environment embodies descends from it. (Already a node in this graph, admitted at Scheme's expansion; proposed here so the link is judged on this parent's documents.)
raw_candidates.source_title: The Early History of Smalltalk (Kay, HOPL-II, 1993)
raw_candidates.definition: John McCarthy's Lisp (1960): symbolic computation as interactive evaluation over a uniform data structure, with garbage collection and a resident image of definitions - the environment model Smalltalk inherits.

raw_candidates.name: Sketchpad
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Named first in Kay's dedication of the four great conceptions: Sketchpad's master drawings and their instances are the object idea in working form - a master changed once changes every instance - and its direct manipulation of visible objects is the interaction premise of the Smalltalk environment. Kay names Sketchpad as a direct inspiration for object-oriented programming and Smalltalk.
raw_candidates.source_title: Sketchpad (Sutherland, 1963) - masters and instances, constraints, direct manipulation
raw_candidates.definition: Ivan Sutherland's Sketchpad (MIT PhD thesis, 1963): interactive drawing on a display with a light pen, organized around master drawings and their occurrences (instances), with geometric constraints maintained by the system - the first working form of the master/instance relation and of direct manipulation.

raw_candidates.definition: Trygve Reenskaug's Model-View-Controller notes (Xerox PARC, May and December 1979): a Model as the active representation of a domain abstraction, Views as its visual representations, and Controllers/Editors coordinating user input - the architectural pattern first implemented in the Smalltalk-80 class library.

candidate.name: Alto

candidate.definition: The Data General Nova (1969): the 16-bit minicomputer on which the first Smalltalk-72 interpreter ran in October 1972, before the port to the Xerox Alto in April 1973.

candidate.name: BitBlt

candidate.name: Lisp

candidate.source_title: The Early History of Smalltalk (Kay, HOPL-II, 1993)
candidate.definition: The Burroughs B5000 (1961): a stack-architecture computer designed for ALGOL - segmented virtual memory, descriptors, byte-coded HLL execution - whose storage ideas Kay carried into the FLEX machine experiments.

candidate.source_title: The Early History of Smalltalk (Kay, HOPL-II, 1993) - ACM record
candidate.definition: Planner (Carl Hewitt, MIT, 1969): a pattern-directed invocation language - assertions and goals invoking procedures by pattern match - among the documented influences on Smalltalk's original design.

candidate.source_title: The Early History of Smalltalk (Kay, HOPL-II, 1993)
candidate.definition: The GENIE operating system (Berkeley, for the SDS 940; Butler Lampson and colleagues, c. 1966): a time-sharing system whose storage-purging discipline - keep core clean by continuously writing out dirty objects - Kay cites as an ingredient of OOZE.

raw_candidates.name: Serial-order recurrent network (Jordan, 1986)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The direct ancestor, modified - in the paper's own abstract: 'The current report develops a proposal along these lines first described by Jordan (1986) which involves the use of recurrent links in order to provide networks with a dynamic memory.' Jordan's network (the paper's Figure 1) feeds OUTPUT patterns back through state/plan units; Elman's modification copies the HIDDEN-unit pattern back as context units, so the memory is the network's own learned internal representation rather than its behavior.
raw_candidates.source_title: Serial Order: A Parallel Distributed Processing Approach (Jordan, 1986; ICS Report 8604, UCSD Institute for Cognitive Science)
raw_candidates.definition: Jordan's serial-order network (ICS Report 8604, UCSD, 1986): a recurrent network for producing sequences, in which plan units and feedback from the output layer ('state units') give the network a context for the next element - the first PDP proposal for dynamic memory through recurrence.

raw_candidates.name: Time-delay neural network (Waibel et al., 1989)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: The strongest form of the incumbent approach the paper argues against: the parent cites Waibel et al. (1987, ATR TR-I-0006 - the report version of the TDNN) among the time-delay designs in which time is laid out spatially over tapped delay lines, the representation strategy the recurrent proposal replaces.
raw_candidates.source_title: Finding Structure in Time (Elman, 1990)
raw_candidates.definition: Time-delay neural network (Waibel et al., 1989; ATR report 1987): a feedforward network whose units receive inputs over a window of time delays, learning shift-invariant temporal features (phoneme recognition) - time represented as space.

raw_candidates.name: Concentrating partial information in a recurrent network (Tank & Hopfield, 1987)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: One of the recurrent proposals the paper's Section 2 surveys (Tank & Hopfield, 1987): recurrent dynamics used to accumulate partial information over time - part of the small 1986-88 recurrent literature the parent situates itself in, though the parent modifies Jordan's design, not this one.
raw_candidates.source_title: Finding Structure in Time (Elman, 1990)
raw_candidates.definition: Tank & Hopfield (1987): a recurrent (Hopfield-style) network that concentrates partial, time-arriving information into a collective decision - recurrence as analog accumulation.

raw_candidates.name: Recurrent backpropagation (Pineda, 1988)
raw_candidates.causal_claim: Cited in the paper's Section 2 survey of recurrent proposals: Pineda's (1988) algorithm for training recurrent networks - the road the parent conspicuously does not take, since its recurrent connections are fixed at 1.0 and untrained.
raw_candidates.source_title: Finding Structure in Time (Elman, 1990)
raw_candidates.definition: Recurrent backpropagation (Pineda, 1988): a generalization of backpropagation that computes gradients for recurrent networks by solving for the fixed point of the network's dynamics.
